bio.en: Casey Winters is a growth and product strategist who has led growth or advised companies including Grubhub, Pinterest, Reddit, Eventbrite (as CPO), Canva, Airbnb, Tinder, and Thumbtack, and was the first repeat guest on Lenny's Podcast.
bio.zh: Casey Winters 是一位增长与产品战略专家，曾领导或与 Grubhub、Pinterest、Reddit、Eventbrite（任 CPO）、Canva、Airbnb、Tinder、Thumbtack 等公司合作或提供顾问，并且是 Lenny 播客第一个返场嘉宾。

summary.en: Casey warns of the "zero interest rate phenomenon product manager" — PMs trained in an era of abundant funding who over-rely on frameworks and research instead of shipping and using judgment. He argues the real PM job (making high-leverage decisions under uncertainty) is AI-resistant, while AI is best used for tedious non-core work. On founder intuition vs team expertise, founders should direct until employees prove they surpass them, then delegate. The episode also breaks down network effects (direct, cross-side, data) and why Grubhub lost to DoorDash despite strong network effects: it underestimated a structurally unprofitable but market-rewarded disruptor. Finally, he explains why consumer subscription businesses are brutally hard (no net dollar retention) and why marketplaces adding SaaS tools beat SaaS tools adding marketplaces.
summary.zh: Casey 警告了"零利率现象产品经理"——那些在资金充沛年代被训练出来、过度依赖框架和研究、而不是发布和使用判断的 PM。他主张真正的 PM 工作（在不确定性下做高杠杆决定）是抗 AI 的，而 AI 最好用于琐碎的非核心活。在创始人直觉 vs 团队专业上，创始人应该指挥，直到员工证明他们超越自己，然后授权。节目还拆解了网络效应（直接、跨边、数据），以及为什么 Grubhub 尽管有强网络效应还是输给 DoorDash：它低估了一个结构亏损但被市场奖励的颠覆者。最后，他解释了为什么消费订阅生意极其难（没有净收入留存率），以及为什么市场加 SaaS 工具胜过 SaaS 工具加市场。

turns.speaker: Casey Winters
turns.en: Every new person on the product team is acting like they work at Google and have these infinite resources and infinite time to make sure everything is perfect. It became such this focus on the right way of doing product management that no one's taken any risk. I felt like, oh, am I responsible for this? I've created a bunch of frameworks on Reforge. I'm onboarding these new PMs. Is this my fault? At Reforge, we're building frameworks that are tools in a toolkit. You pull them out when relevant. They're not a coloring book to stay inside the lines of.
turns.zh: 产品团队里每个新人，都表现得像在 Google 工作一样，有无限的资源、无限的时间去把一切都做到完美。这变成了一种对"做产品管理正确方式"的执念，以至于没人敢冒任何风险。我当时就想，哦，这该不会是我的责任吧？我在 Reforge 上搞了一堆框架。我在带这些新 PM 入职。这是我的错吗？在 Reforge，我们建的是工具箱里的工具。相关的时侯你把它抽出来用。它们不是一本让你待在框框里涂色的填色书。

turns.speaker: Casey Winters
turns.en: Thanks, Lenny. Great to be here.
turns.zh: 谢谢 Lenny。很高兴来到这里。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You are the first ever return guest to my podcast. How does that feel?
turns.zh: 你是我播客有史以来第一个返场嘉宾。感觉怎么样？

turns.speaker: Casey Winters
turns.en: I feel honored, perhaps a bit unworthy, but I'll go with it.
turns.zh: 我感到荣幸，也许还有点受之有愧，但我就接着收下了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Well, you're both worthy and I'm honored as well. Thanks for joining me again. I have a lot of stuff that I want to chat about, but first of all, I'm just curious, what are you up to these days? I know you left Eventbrite as CPO, I know you're doing a few advisorships with startups, but how are you spending your days, and what do you think is next for Casey Winters?
turns.zh: 嗯，你配得上，我也很荣幸。再次谢谢你来。我有好多想聊的，但首先我好奇，你最近在忙什么？我知道你离开了 Eventbrite 的 CPO 岗位，知道你在给几家初创做顾问，但你日子是怎么过的？Casey Winters 接下来想往哪走？

turns.speaker: Casey Winters
turns.en: I'm still spending some time with Whatnot and Eventbrite as advisors. I stepped back from the CPO of Eventbrite in October, but still working on some long-term marketplace strategy stuff, some growth strategy stuff. I'm on the board of a company called Beek, which is like Netflix for audio in Latin America, and I'm doing some angel investing in marketplaces in what I call tech debt as a service, which is what are startups that are building out things that were hard for my teams in the past to build or maintain inside previous companies? The other thing I'm working on is revamping the product strategy program for Reforge. I got some things keeping me busy, but definitely not as busy as I was last year.
turns.zh: 我还在以顾问身份花些时间在 Whatnot 和 Eventbrite 上。我十月退下了 Eventbrite 的 CPO，但还在做一些长期的市场策略、增长策略的事。我在一家叫 Beek 的公司董事会里，它像是拉美地区的"音频版 Netflix"，我还在一些市场类公司里做天使投资，我称之为"技术债即服务"——也就是那些在搭建以前我团队很难在之前公司里建起来或维护的东西的初创。另一件我在做的事，是重塑 Reforge 的产品战略项目。有些事让我忙，但肯定没去年那么忙。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This is like a rare, free agent Case Winters time. Should people reach out if they're interested in maybe working with you? What's your advice for people listening?
turns.zh: 这像是罕见的、自由身的 Case Winters 时期。如果有人有兴趣合作，应该联系你吗？你对听众的建议是什么？

turns.speaker: Casey Winters
turns.en: Yeah. I always love seeing how I can help companies. Everyone should err on the side of reaching out and seeing if I have time to help, if there's something they think I can help with. I love talking to startups, so yeah, absolutely. I can't promise anything, but yeah, I just love talking to people about this stuff.
turns.zh: 对。我一直喜欢看我能怎么帮到公司。每个人都应该偏向主动联系、看我有没有时间帮忙，如果有什么他们觉得我能帮上的。我超爱跟初创聊，所以是的，绝对可以。我没法保证什么，但我就是爱跟人聊这些事。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. We'll point people to how to get in touch with you at the end of the episode, and it'll be in the show notes too. Talking about the CPO role, you're at Eventbrite. You're a CPO. It reminds me of a post you wrote about how hard the CPO role is. There's some quotes that I recall in your post about how, one, if you ever ask a CPO, chief product officer how they're doing, no one's ever going to say, "I'm crushing it right now."
turns.zh: 太棒了。我们会在节目结尾告诉大家怎么联系你，也会放在节目简介里。说到 CPO 这个角色，你在 Eventbrite。你是 CPO。这让我想起你写的一篇关于 CPO 这角色有多难的文章。我记得你文章里有几句引语，一是，如果你问一个 CPO（首席产品官）"最近怎么样"，从来没人会说"我现在正碾压一切"。

turns.speaker: Casey Winters
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Then there's this other quote about how you basically, as a CPO, just try to put some points on the board before you inevitably get fired. Why is that? Why do you find that, and do you still believe that to be true after leaving that role?
turns.zh: 然后还有另一句，大概是说，作为 CPO，你基本就是抢在 inevitable 被炒之前，先往记分牌上挂几分。为什么？你怎么看这个，离开那个角色之后你还信这个吗？

turns.speaker: Casey Winters
turns.en: Yeah, I would say I still believe those things I said. It was funny. A product leader who will remain nameless emailed me when I hit year three at Eventbrite, and they said, "Congrats. You didn't get fired after two years. What's your secret?" I think it's very hard to keep product-market fit as a CPO within a company for a long time. The needs of the business shift over time, and of course, we all have different strengths and weaknesses in our game. No one's perfect at everything. In general, as an executive, it's just impossible to do everything perfectly, and any little misstep, mistake, or something you just missed can blow up in a major way. (00:06:33): Frequently, CEOs have visions that can change and get misaligned with the product leader. Also, with leadership roles, you don't get put on a PIP. If a CEO loses confidence, it's over immediately. Nothing like that happened at Eventbrite. I started to see that the areas of leverage for a product leader were just less in my wheelhouse over time. I just talked to my boss about it, and we worked out something where I continue to advise on the things that I'm uniquely good at, and find other people who are better at some of these other things that were maybe more important at the time. (00:07:09): Yeah, I'd say it's a really hard role, or a really challenging role. It can be a lot of fun. I learned a lot from doing it, but yeah, I still believe, and I think I've still yet to hear someone say they've really crushed it.
turns.zh: 对，我会说我还信我说的那些。有意思。有个产品负责人——名字不提了——在我 Eventbrite 干到第三年的时候给我发了封邮件，说"恭喜。你两年没被炒。你的秘诀是什么？"我觉得，作为一个 CPO，要在一家公司里长期保持产品市场契合非常难。业务的需求随着时间会变，当然，我们每个人都有自己游戏里的长处和短处。没有人在一切上完美。总体上，作为高管，要把每件事都做完美根本不可能，而任何一点小失策、小错误，或者你刚好漏掉的东西，都可能炸成大问题。（00:06:33）经常，CEO 的愿景会变、会跟产品负责人错位。还有，在领导岗位上，你不会先被 PIP（绩效改进计划）。如果 CEO 失去信心，立刻就完了。Eventbrite 没发生那种事。我开始看到，产品负责人的杠杆点，随着时间越来越不在我的舒适区里。我就跟我的老板聊了，我们商量出一个方案：我继续在我特别擅长的那些事上做顾问，去找其他更擅长某些当时可能更重要的事的人。（00:07:09）对，我会说这是个真的很难、非常挑战的角色。它也可以很有意思。我从里面学到很多，但对的，我还信，而且我觉得我至今还没听过有人说自己真的碾压了一切。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there anything that you learned from that experience to have survived in that role for three years? I imagine you have a lot of skills and you were very valuable to the company, but I don't know, for someone in that's role maybe right now, just like, "Here's something that I did that maybe you should do."
turns.zh: 有没有你从那个经历里学到的、让你在那个角色上活了三年的东西？我猜你有一堆技能、对公司很有价值，但我不知道，对现在正处在这个角色的人，就"这是我做过、也许你该做的事"。

turns.speaker: Casey Winters
turns.en: The first one I can think of is a big change from being a product leader to a CPO or something equivalent is you're actually a company exec first and a product exec second. I think some mistakes I made early that I corrected successfully is you want to show that you are caring and paying attention to the overall business first before just taking care of your own product designers, product managers, researchers, whoever. That's advice I found myself doling out to other product leaders a lot more now that I've gone through it. You have to not only truly care, but create the perception that you care about sales, about marketing, about legal, et cetera. Because first and foremost, you're expected to lead the business at that level, so I think that's something that I think is really important. (00:08:35): I think something else is really trying to diagnose, without as much bias as possible, where are the strengths and weaknesses of your team? Where are the strengths and weaknesses of your product? Lay that out with your peers and say, "Here's where we are. Here's where I think we need to go. Here's the timeline on which I'm going to work to get us there." Because I think product's such a confusing discipline for people who aren't in it, like a sales leader, many CEOs, a marketing leader, that they don't necessarily know what great looks like. (00:09:14): The things they know about great leadership, they don't know if you know those things, so you have to make it really clear, "Yeah, I know our OKRs are not as quantitative as they should be yet. That's because this team isn't ready for X, Y, and Z. This is where we're going to get them to, but it's going to take some time." One of the things we did at Eventbrite that I thought was really helpful is, when you go public, you tend to rotate over your executive team and get public company execs versus startup execs. A few of us were new, and it's just like, "Hey, let's do a deep dive on product. Let's do a deep dive on customer support. Where's it at right now? What do you feel like your job is? What do you feel like are the issues you're facing? Where do you want to take it over the next three to five years? Then, let's talk about it." (00:09:57): Just forcing you to write it all down is really helpful, but then it forces you to explain it. It helps the rest of the executive team get better company execs because now they really understand product a lot more deeply, or understand finance a lot more deeply, whatever the function is.
turns.zh: 我第一个能想到的，是从产品负责人到 CPO 或同等角色的一大转变：你其实首先是个公司高管，其次才是个产品高管。我觉得我早期犯过、后来成功改正的错误是：你得先表现出你在关心、在注意整体业务，然后才去照顾你自己的产品设计师、产品经理、研究员，谁谁谁。这是我走过来之后，现在更频繁地给其他产品负责人提的建议。你不只是真得关心，还得营造出你在关心销售、关心营销、关心法务等等的观感。因为首先，在那个层级你是被期待领导业务的，所以我觉得这点真的很重要。（00:08:35）我觉得另一件是，真的尽量不带那么多偏见地去诊断：你团队的长处和短处在哪？你产品的长处和短处在哪？跟你的同侪摊开来讲："我们在这。我觉得我们要去那。我打算在这个时间线上把我们带到那。"因为我觉得产品对不在行的人来说太容易困惑了，比如销售负责人、很多 CEO、营销负责人，他们不一定知道"好"长什么样。（00:09:14）他们知道那些好领导的事，但他们不知道你知不知道那些事，所以你得说得很清楚："对，我知道我们的 OKR 还该更量化。那是因为这个团队还没准备好 X、Y、Z。这是我们打算带他们到的地方，但需要点时间。"我们在 Eventbrite 做的一件我觉得真有帮助的事：当你上市，你往往会轮换你的高管团队，换成上市公司高管而非初创高管。我们几个是新人，然后就像"嘿，来对产品做个深潜。来对客户支持做个深潜。现在到哪了？你觉得你的工作是什么？你觉得你面对的问题是什么？未来三到五年你想把它带到哪？然后我们聊。"（00:09:57）光是逼你全写下来就很有帮助，但接着它逼你解释。它帮其余的高管团队成为更好的公司高管，因为他们现在真的更深地理解了产品、或者更深地理解了财务，无论哪个职能。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Speaking of gaps and opportunities for people in the company to level up, you've been highlighting this trend that I thought was really interesting, something you call the zero interest rate phenomenon product manager. Can you talk about what that is and what you've been noticing?
turns.zh: 说到公司里人往上补的缺口和机会，你一直在强调一个我觉得很有意思的趋势，你所谓的"零利率现象产品经理"。你能讲讲那是什么、你注意到了什么？

turns.speaker: Casey Winters
turns.en: Yeah, sure thing. This is something I started noticing while managing PMs and product designers at Eventbrite, and it's now coming up with Whatnot as I help them hire new PMs, is the environment in which a lot of product managers have come up is very distorted from when you and I started doing this kind of work. I think we used to always describe PMs as this gang of misfits. We all started in all different functions. We all had different strengths and weaknesses, and the PM team gained as a whole from that diversity of skills and previous experiences. (00:11:12): What I noticed is, when we started doing product reviews at Eventbrite, if there was any sort of uncertainty in a problem or a solution, the product manager, instead of shipping to learn, would talk about all this research they have to do to really learn the problems, really learn the solution. (00:11:30): My feedback would be like, no, user research is a scarce resource. We have to reserve it for the areas that have extreme uncertainty and high leverage for getting to certain, so if you're redesigning the login page for Eventbrite, you don't need to use that resource to learn what to do. Just go see what FANG and the top unicorns did. They probably did a good job, and even if they didn't, all of our customers also use those products, so they're going to be familiar with us copying any approach that they've taken. (00:12:05): I think we sort of forgot in the industry that many times, the fastest way to learn is to ship, so that if you actually get them to skip research and just go look at competitors, another thing I was noticing is I'd get a list of options other companies have done, but there would be no analysis of why those companies chose different options and what's most applicable for us. (00:12:31): It got me thinking, okay, every new person on the product team is acting like they work at Google and have these infinite resources and infinite time to make sure everything is perfect. It became such this focus on the right way of doing product management that no one's taken any risk. I felt like, oh, am I responsible for this? I've created a bunch of frameworks on Reforge. I'm onboarding these new PMs. Is this my fault? At Reforge, we're building frameworks that are tools in a toolkit. You pull them out when relevant. They're not a coloring book to stay inside the lines of. (00:13:10): At one point, I got so fed up, I wrote an internal blog post, and I called it On Best Practices and Breakfast Rituals. I talked about how there were these articles about the morning habits of the most successful people, and if you try to do all those things, it'd take you like six hours every morning. There was this article, I think it was on Business Insider or something, about this futurist at Google. He talked about all the pills and food he eats for breakfast every morning to try to live longer. The reporter estimated that it cost him one million a year to have these habits, so I was like, "Hey, I want to make it clear. At Eventbrite, we don't have that much money. We don't have that much time. There's no framework that allows you to not use your brain at this company and just follow some sort of process for success in this profession." (00:14:02): I adopted this thing into a public blog post that's on my blog now, but now that I've had some time outside of Eventbrite, I feel like I at least partially missed the mark on what's really going on. I see this with Whatnot, because one of the things I'm helping them with is interviewing, I see PMs again, which I haven't done in a while. It's fascinating interviewing a PM or managers early in their career because Whatnot is a startup, and you know better than most of us as a former founder of one, startups typically require us to wear lots of hats. You have to write SQL. You have to talk directly to customers. You have to prep marketing and sales. Most importantly, you have to make a lot of decisions under uncertainty, which you wouldn't necessarily expect a PM to do at, say, a Google, but it all boils down to using your brain in different ways. (00:14:54): Lisa, who's on our legal team, she called Eventbrite a public startup because the pandemic basically erased her business and we had to build it back from scratch. Now that I'm doing these interviews, and whether they come from a small startup, a unicorn, or a public company, they all sort of look the same because there's been so much funding to all these companies. Every company's been acting like they're Google with Google margins, meaning a lot of engineering support, a lot of design support, a lot of research support, lots of analysts around them. (00:15:22): They actually seem pretty ill-prepared for a real startup, or even a public company with some uncertainty around it like Eventbrite, so you start getting these weird responses in the interview process. You ask them to solve a problem and they'd say things like, "I can't even begin to come up with solutions until I see all the data and talk to customers." I'm like, "Yeah, I get that's something you would normally do if you took the job, but you don't have the data. You can't talk to customers. Make a decision now. What would you do? I want to see how creative you are. I want to see how much you're intuiting about the real problem and solution," and they can't really answer. (00:15:56): Then my follow-up, which I don't ask, but what I really want to ask is like, "When's the last time you used your brain versus followed a process someone else designed at your company?" Because I want the former, not the latter.
turns.zh: 对，当然。这是我管 Eventbrite 的 PM 和产品设计师时注意到的，现在帮 Whatnot 招新 PM 时也冒出来了：很多产品经理成长起来的环境，跟你我开始干这行时已经非常扭曲了。我觉得我们以前总把 PM 描述成一群"不合群的人"。我们都从不同的职能起步。我们各有长短，而 PM 团队整体上从那种技能和过往经验的多样性中获益。（00:11:12）我注意到的是，当我们在 Eventbrite 做产品评审时，如果问题或方案有任何不确定性，产品经理不是"先发布、再学习"，而是会讲他们得做多少研究才能真正搞懂问题、搞懂方案。（00:11:30）我的反馈会是：不，用户研究是稀缺资源。我们得把它留给那些极端不确定、而且杠杆很高、能让你确定下来的领域，所以如果你在重做 Eventbrite 的登录页，你不需要用那个资源去学该做什么。直接去看 FANG（Facebook、Amazon、Netflix、Google）和顶级独角兽做了什么。他们大概做得不错，就算没做好，我们所有客户也用那些产品，所以他们会对我们抄任何他们用过的方式感到熟悉。（00:12:05）我觉得行业里我们某种程度上忘了：很多次，最快的学习方式是发布，所以如果你真让他们跳过研究、直接去看竞品，我注意到的另一件事是：我会收到一张别的公司做过的选项清单，但对那些公司为什么选不同选项、什么对我们最适用，完全没有分析。（00:12:31）这让我想，好吧，产品团队每个新人，都表现得像在 Google 工作、有无限资源和无限时间去把一切做完美。这变成了一种对"做产品管理正确方式"的执念，以至于没人冒任何风险。我当时就想，哦，这该不会是我的责任吧？我在 Reforge 搞了一堆框架。我在带这些新 PM 入职。这是我的错吗？在 Reforge，我们建的是工具箱里的工具。相关的时侯抽出来用。它们不是一本让你待在框框里涂色的填色书。（00:13:10）有阵子我受够了，写了篇内部博客，叫《论最佳实践与早餐仪式》。我聊了那些关于"最成功的人早晨习惯"的文章，如果你试图全做，每天早上得花你六小时。有篇文章，我记得是在 Business Insider 还是哪，讲 Google 一个未来学家。他讲了他每天早上为了活得长吃的所有药丸和食物。记者估出来光这些习惯一年就得花他一百万。所以我就说："嘿，我想说清楚。在 Eventbrite，我们没那么多钱。我们没那么多时间。这个公司里没有任何框架能让你不用动脑、只要跟着某个流程就能成功。"（00:14:02）我把这东西改成了一篇公开博客，现在在我博客上，但既然我离开 Eventbrite 有段时间了，我觉得我至少部分没说中真正在发生的事。我在 Whatnot 看到这个，因为我帮他们的一件事是面试，我又见到 PM 了，好一阵没见了。面试一个早期职业的 PM 或经理特别有意思，因为 Whatnot 是初创，而你作为一家初创的前创始人比我们大多数人都更懂：初创通常要求我们戴很多帽子。你得写 SQL。你得直接跟客户聊。你得给营销和销售做准备。最重要的是，你得在不确定性下做大量决定——你不一定会期待一个 Google 的 PM 做这个，但说到底，就是用不同方式动你的脑子。（00:14:54）Lisa，我们法务团队的，她叫 Eventbrite 一个"上市初创"，因为疫情基本抹掉了她的业务，我们得从零重建。既然我在做这些面试，无论他们来自小初创、独角兽还是上市公司，他们看起来都差不多，因为给所有这些公司的钱都太多了。每家公司都表现得像它们是有着 Google 级别利润率的 Google，意思是大量工程支持、大量设计支持、大量研究支持、身边一堆分析师。（00:15:22）他们其实对一个真初创、甚至对一个像 Eventbrite 那样带点不确定性的上市公司，准备得相当不足，所以面试里你开始得到这些怪回答。你让他们解决一个问题，他们会说"在我看到所有数据、跟客户聊过之前，我连想方案都无从下手。"我就想"对，我知道如果你接了这活，你通常会那么做，但你现在没数据。你不能跟客户聊。现在做个决定。你会怎么做？我想看你多有创意。我想看你多能直觉到真正的问题和方案"，而他们答不上来。（00:15:56）然后我的追问——我没真问，但我真想问的是："你上一次用你脑子、而不是跟着别人在公司设计的流程走，是什么时候？"因为我想要前者，不是后者。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow. Amazing. There's a lot of things I want to dig into here. I was going to ask why you call it zero interest rate phenomenon, but I think what I'm hearing is it's when interest rates are zero, everyone's got a lot of money, things are going great. Everyone looks like they're killing it, successful. Everyone thinks they've got it all figured out, and then when that goes away, it's like, "Oh, shit. Maybe not so."
turns.zh: 哇。太精彩了。这里有很多我想深挖。我本来想问你为什么叫它"零利率现象"，但我想我听到的是：当利率是零，大家都有很多钱，一切很好。每个人都看起来在碾压、在成功。每个人都觉得他们全搞明白了，然后当那个消失，就像"哦，糟了。也许不是那么回事。"

turns.speaker: Casey Winters
turns.en: Then also, I think zero interest rates allowed every startup to operate like it was a public company with billions of dollars. That's going to go away over the next five years, and it sort of takes us back to what product management used to be like, which was you didn't have all these resources around. You didn't have all this time to figure it out because if you don't figure it out now and make it work, you may run out of funding, right?
turns.zh: 还有，我觉得零利率让每个初创都能像个有几十亿美金的上市公司那样运作。这会在未来五年消失，把我们带回产品管理以前的样子——也就是你身边没有所有那些资源。你没有所有时间去想明白，因为如果你现在不想明白、不把它做起来，你可能就把融资烧光了，对吧？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. Like a very concrete thing that's changed as a lot of research teams have been laid off because they grew really large and companies found, "Maybe we need don't need the ..." Like, "Of all the things we can cut, it's probably an area we can cut."
turns.zh: 对。就像个很具体的变化：很多研究团队被裁了，因为他们长太大，公司发现"也许我们不需要那个……"就像"所有能砍的东西里，那大概是我们能砍的一个领域。"

turns.speaker: Casey Winters
turns.en: Yeah, for sure.
turns.zh: 对，当然。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There's probably PMs listening to this wondering, "Shoot, am I one of these? Am I just following a bunch of frameworks?" What's your advice for someone that may fear that, "Oh, shoot. This is maybe who I am and I don't want to necessarily be this"? What could they maybe do?
turns.zh: 大概有 PM 在听这个，心想"糟了，我是其中一个吗？我是不是就跟着一堆框架走？"对于那些可能害怕"糟了，这也许就是我、而我不想一定是这样"的人，你的建议是什么？他们也许能做什么？

turns.speaker: Casey Winters
turns.en: I always advise going to companies where you can learn quickly and try things. I think it's certainly okay to learn a bunch of frameworks. There's a reason I've invested a ton of time in Reforge because I think it actually really does help people to see how other people build things in a way that they can scale it to their other companies, but you have to understand that the job is not to follow the process. The job is not to learn every framework possible. The job is to figure out how to add value to customers that translates into value to the business. Just reorient your North Star, if you've gotten away from that. (00:17:53): When I joined Eventbrite, there was this team that didn't ship anything in a quarter. I went to the designer who I knew, and I know that he likes to get stuff out there and likes to get feedback. I was like, "Dude, you didn't ship anything. How could you have gone the entire quarter, not shipped any of your designs and felt that that was okay? If you didn't feel it was okay, why did you censor yourself? Come to me. Tell me why this team is not letting you ship. There's just no way you can get better as a designer. There's no way you can have the impact on the company. There's no way you can have an impact on our users." Those are some things that come to mind to that question.
turns.zh: 我总建议去那些你能快速学习、试东西的公司。我觉得学一堆框架当然 OK。我投了大量时间在 Reforge 是有原因的，因为我觉得它真的帮人看到别人怎么建东西，从而能扩展到他们其他公司，但你必须理解：这工作不是跟着流程走。这工作不是学所有可能的框架。这工作是想出怎么给客户加价值、并转化成对业务的价值。如果你偏离了，重新对准你的北极星。（00:17:53）我加入 Eventbrite 时，有个团队一整个季度什么都没发布。我去找那个我认识的设计师，我知道他喜欢把东西发出去、喜欢拿反馈。我说"兄弟，你什么都没发。你怎么能整季都没发任何一个你的设计、还觉得那 OK？如果你觉得不 OK，你为什么自我审查？来找我。告诉我为什么这团队不让你发。你作为一个设计师根本不可能变好。你不可能对公司有影响。你不可能对我们的用户有影响。"那些是想到这个问题时冒出来的事。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: If you're a PM on a team that maybe isn't shipping, maybe is overusing research, do you have any advice of just like when it makes sense to invest in research? Say you have the resources, is there a rule of thumb you have of like, "Okay. Let's actually spend the time on this verse not"?
turns.zh: 如果你是一个在也许不发布、也许过度用研究的团队里的 PM，你有没有什么建议，就关于什么时候值得投研究？假设你有资源，你有没有个经验法则，像"好，这块我们真的花时间，那块不"？

turns.speaker: Casey Winters
turns.en: I think about it a little bit, depending on the type of job you have and the types of customers you have. The more scale you have tends to be you have less sophisticated customers because you're generally like a consumer thing where the customers are rational. They're not experts. That's generally where you just try things. You measure the impact they have, and you only really bring in USEARCH, research when the impact seems confusing, but you can run experiments. You can get data really easily, so bias towards getting stuff out there and seeing what users respond to.
turns.zh: 我会稍微想一下，看你是什么类型的工作、什么类型的客户。规模越大，往往你的客户越不老练，因为你一般是消费类东西，客户是理性的。他们不是专家。那通常是你直接试东西的地方。你衡量它们的影响，你真的只在影响看起来令人困惑时才引入用户研究，但你能跑实验。你能很容易拿到数据，所以偏向把东西发出去、看用户怎么反应。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: In consumer product.
turns.zh: 在消费产品上。

turns.speaker: Casey Winters
turns.en: Right.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Interesting.
turns.zh: 有意思。

turns.speaker: Casey Winters
turns.en: If you're super enterprise, it's the opposite. Each customer, first off, is sophisticated and tend to be rational. They're paying you like six figures or more, and you could talk to the customers and sales, who knows the customers really well directly, and they tell you want they want. They tell you what they're willing to pay for. You build it. They pay you. Bing, bang, boom. It's not, obviously, as simple as that, but you're basically doing the research directly with the customer and with the sales team, and translating that into things that are strategic to the business. (00:20:02): I would say those are the two extremes probably most people are familiar with, but we now have a lot of companies in the middle, where they have more customers. Those customers are more sophisticated. They're consumers. They're maybe employees at companies, or they're small businesses. That's where you have to be more nuanced. This, of course, is where Eventbrite was on, "Hey, when do I really lean in on research? When do I lean in on data? When do I pay attention to internal feedback? (00:20:29): " For Eventbrite, we really tried to focus research on the B2B side of Eventbrite, where the problems seemed big, but not well-defined enough. Or that problem's well-defined, but we just really don't feel like we have the right solution yet. If research is going to be a scarce resource inside the company, which I think it will in most places, you have to figure out where it's a high-leverage area, which means either really big problem, we don't understand it well enough, or we know the problem's big. We understand it well, but we're just not sure if our solution's going to, in any way, hit the mark.
turns.zh: 如果你是完全的企业级，正好相反。每个客户，首先就老练、理性。他们付你六位数或更多，你能跟客户和销售聊——销售很懂客户——他们直接告诉你想要什么。他们告诉你愿意付什么。你建。他们付你。bing、bang、boom。当然没那么简单，但你基本是直接跟客户、跟销售团队做研究，再把它翻译成对业务有战略意义的东西。（00:20:02）我会说那两个极端大概是大多数人熟悉的，但我们现在有很多中间的公司，他们客户更多。那些客户更老练。他们是消费者。他们也许是公司的员工，或者是小企业。那才是你得更有分寸的地方。当然，Eventbrite 就在那，"嘿，我什么时候真的要压上研究？什么时候压上数据？什么时候留意内部反馈？"（00:20:29）对 Eventbrite，我们真试着把研究聚焦在 B2B 那侧，那里问题看起来大、但定义得不够好。或者问题定义得好，但我们就是真觉得还没对的方案。如果研究在公司里是稀缺资源——我觉得大多数地方都是——你得想清楚哪里是高杠杆区域，也就是要么问题真的很大、我们理解得不够，要么我们知道问题大、理解得好，但我们就是不确定方案会不会在任何意义上命中目标。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Makes me think about some of the best researchers I've worked with, and they often tell me like, "We don't need to do research on this. We have enough information. We have other things we should be doing."
turns.zh: 让我想到我合作过的一些最好的研究员，他们常跟我说"这个我们不需要做研究。我们有足够信息。我们有更该做的事。"

turns.speaker: Casey Winters
turns.en: I love it when they say that. Yes.
turns.zh: 他们那么说的时候我超爱。对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. This would have been a really good segue to another topic I want to talk about, which is around gut instincts versus team expertise, which we're going to get to, but I have a couple more questions along these lines.
turns.zh: 对。这本来能很好地过渡到我想聊的另一个话题，关于直觉 vs 团队专业，我们待会会到，但我还有几个顺着这个方向的问题。

turns.speaker: Casey Winters
turns.en: Sure.
turns.zh: 当然。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You talked about interviewing PMs at Whatnot. Can you actually describe Whatnot? Just because you mentioned it a couple times, just so people know what we're talking about here.
turns.zh: 你聊了在 Whatnot 面试 PM。你能实际描述一下 Whatnot 吗？就因为你提了几次，让人知道我们在聊什么。

turns.speaker: Casey Winters
turns.en: Oh, sure. Whatnot's a livestreaming marketplace, mostly focused on the collectibles market. Sellers, whether it's like baseball cards, or women's handbags, or sneakers, they'll go live on video and show you the products they have that they're selling. People that are watching the stream can engage with the sellers and bid on different items, so kind of like Twitch meets eBay would be a good way to describe it.
turns.zh: 哦，当然。Whatnot 是个直播 marketplace（市场），主要聚焦收藏品市场。卖家，不管是棒球卡、女包还是球鞋，他们会开视频直播，给你看他们要卖的产品。看直播的人能跟卖家互动、对不同物品竞拍，所以大概可以描述为 Twitch 遇见 eBay。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome, awesome. I'll just mention, I'm a tiny angel investor in that company.
turns.zh: 太棒了，太棒了。我就提一句，我是那家公司的一个小天使投资人。

turns.speaker: Casey Winters
turns.en: Oh, that's why you brought it up. Okay, I get it.
turns.zh: 哦，难怪你提它。好，我懂了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, I just wanted to make sure people understood what this word was because it's like a fun word, Whatnot. What I wanted to actually get to is you said you were interviewing a lot of project managers for them.
turns.zh: 对，我只是想确保大家理解这个词是什么，因为 Whatnot 是个好玩的词。我真正想聊的是，你说你在帮他们面了很多项目经理（PM）。

turns.speaker: Casey Winters
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What is your approach to interviewing PMs? What do you find is a really good signal for someone that's going to be successful?
turns.zh: 你面 PM 的方法是什么？你发现什么是一个会成功的人真正好的信号？

turns.speaker: Casey Winters
turns.en: I feel like the whole thing's gotten so performative. It's like interviewing is handing out Oscars based on who's prepared the best tell me about a time response, versus actually assessing who can do the job we're hiring for. It's like most PMs are better PM interviewers than PMs now. There's this quote from a movie called The Way of the Gun. I don't know if you've ever seen it.
turns.zh: 我觉得整件事变得太"表演"了。面试像是根据谁把"讲讲你一次……"准备得最好来发奥斯卡，而不是真的评估谁干得了我们招的这个活。现在好像大多数 PM 比 PM 还会面 PM。有部电影叫《枪之道》（The Way of the Gun），不知你看过没。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: No.
turns.zh: 没。

turns.speaker: Casey Winters
turns.en: Benicio del Toro says in it, it's like, "These days, they want to be criminals more than they want to commit crime." I think about that quote a lot when it comes to interviewing. I would say I'm a bit contrarian here in my approach. I don't ask about your work history. I don't care about your perfectly practiced answers. I'm going to give you real scenarios that I expect from the role. I want to hear how you'd approach them. If you can't come up with a few reasonable ideas, figure out how to test them quickly without analyst support or research, I'm just not interested. (00:23:10): I'm not saying this is a perfect approach. Interviewing is a very lossy format, but the more I can see them do the job we're hiring for with questions, whether it's a presentation, a prompt, that gets me the most comfortable that they know the job they're signing up for, that they've shown in a practice scenario they can do it, and they actually enjoyed it in some way.
turns.zh: Benicio del Toro 在里面说，大概是"这年头，他们想当罪犯，胜过想犯罪。"每次想到面试我就想起这句。我会说我在方法上有点反主流。我不问你的工作史。我不在乎你完美练习过的答案。我会给你这个角色里我期待的真实场景。我想听你怎么处理它们。如果你想不出几个合理的点子、想不出怎么在没有分析师支持或研究的情况下快速测它们，我就没兴趣。（00:23:10）我不是说这是完美的方法。面试是个很损（lossy）的形式，但我越能在问题上看到他们做我们招的活——无论是演示还是提示——我就越放心：他们知道签的是什么活、他们在练习场景里展示了能做、而且他们在某方面真的享受。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Are there red flags you look for in these interviews? One is maybe you said of like, "I can't even begin to answer this without research and data." Is there anything else?
turns.zh: 这些面试里你会找什么红旗？一个你说过，也许是"没有研究和数据我连开始回答都不行。"还有别的吗？

turns.speaker: Casey Winters
turns.en: Some things I pay attention to is if they're talking about solutions that are going to take a long time to get signal from, whether it's months and months of engineering time before you actually see the impact on users or the business, I think that's always great. If they're not factoring in the amount of time it will take, in general, is not a good sign, and not thinking a bit more holistically about the types of metrics they expect to improve versus track to make sure they haven't gone down. Those are some things that I pay a lot of attention to.
turns.zh: 我注意的一些事是：如果他们讲的方案要花很久才能拿到信号——不管是几个月几个月的工程时间，你才真正看到对用户或业务的影响——我觉得那总不太好。如果他们总体上不把要花的时间算进去，不是个好信号；不更整体地想想他们预期改善而非只追踪、确保没下滑的指标类型。那些是我很注意的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: How much do you think they're intimidated by being interviewed by Casey Winters? How much do you think that factors in?
turns.zh: 你觉得他们被 Casey Winters 面试，有多被吓到？你觉得那占多大因素？

turns.speaker: Casey Winters
turns.en: I think you overestimate my importance or awareness in the community. I think most people have no idea who I am when they start talking to me.
turns.zh: 我觉得你高估了我在圈子里的重要性或知名度。我觉得大多数人一开始跟我聊时根本不知道我是谁。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Mm-hmm. [inaudible 00:24:25] Another thought is there's this meme that GBT-4, or 5, or 6, or 10 is going to replace product managers, and anytime some new feature comes out, people will put out these videos of, "Oh, look. They're doing all the PM's jobs." What's your take on the future of PM in AI, if any?
turns.zh: 嗯。[听不清 00:24:25]另一个想法是，有个梗说 GPT-4、或 5、或 6、或 10 会取代产品经理，每次出个新功能，人们就发视频"哦看，他们在干 PM 所有的活。"你对 PM 在 AI 里的未来怎么看，如果有的话？

turns.speaker: Casey Winters
turns.en: Well, I think if you thought the PM job was just filling in the latest Reforge or Shreyas framework, and then getting that automatic FANG promotion every year and a half, then yeah, you're going to get replaced by AI. I think the real PM job is the least likely to get replaced over time because you need real subject matter expertise. You need to be trading off a lot of different types of things, and making good decisions for the company and for your customers. (00:25:10): In terms of using AI now as a PM, I'd actually be cautious in the current iteration of the cycle for PMs. It's a tool that's trained on sounding smart rather than always necessarily being smart. I was at Eventbrite the other day, and someone was telling me how they were loving the new Notion AI integration. She asked me if I used it. I said, "No." She's like, "Ah, you totally need to. Hey, go ask it your bio. It's really cool." I said, "All right. Let's just do it on your screen," so she did and my bio said I started my career at Google, and worked on Google Trends, and a bunch of other products, none of which happened. It was just complete nonsense. (00:25:52): It did have some stuff that did happen. It knew I worked at Eventbrite, and it knew I worked at Pinterest and stuff, but half of it was just completely made up. It sounded plausible, but it wasn't actually true. I think where I'm more inclined for PMs to try to get leverage out of something like GPT-4 is a lot of the tedious work that's maybe not their specialty to begin with. If you're not great at Excel or Google Sheets and you need to model something, you can ask it to format something. That'll probably be perfect, or how to get some Zapier integration to work. It probably knows how to do that really well. (00:26:28): I think, at this point, it's a pretty good no-code to low-code tool. It's obviously going to become a lot more than that, but for a lot of these other use cases that people are touting, there's a decent chance, confidently tells you the wrong thing, and that would scare me as a PM.
turns.zh: 嗯，我觉得如果你以为 PM 的活就是填最新的 Reforge 或 Shreyas 框架，然后每一年半自动拿个 FANG 晋升，那对，你会被 AI 取代。我觉得真正的 PM 活是最不容易随时间被取代的，因为你需要真正的领域专长。你需要权衡很多不同类型的东西，为公司和你的客户做好的决定。（00:25:10）关于现在 PM 用 AI，在当下这个周期里我其实会谨慎。它是个被训练成"听起来聪明"、而不一定总是"真聪明"的工具。我前阵子在 Eventbrite，有人跟我讲她多爱新的 Notion AI 集成。她问我用没用。我说"没。"她说"啊，你绝对得用。来，去问它你的 bio。超酷。"我说"行，就在你屏幕上试吧"，所以她试了，我的 bio 说我是谷歌起家、做过 Google Trends 和一堆其他产品，没一个发生过。纯属胡扯。（00:25:52）它确实有部分真发生过的。它知道我在 Eventbrite 工作、知道我在 Pinterest 之类，但一半完全是编的。听着像那么回事，但其实不真。我觉得我更倾向于让 PM 从 GPT-4 这类东西里拿杠杆的地方，是很多本来就不是他们专长的琐碎活。如果你不擅长 Excel 或 Google Sheets、需要建个模型，你可以让它帮你排版。那大概会完美，或者怎么让某个 Zapier 集成跑起来。它大概很懂怎么做那个。（00:26:28）我觉得在当下，它是个相当好的无代码到低代码工具。它显然会变成远超这个的东西，但对人们吹的那些其他用例，它有相当概率自信地告诉你错的东西，那会吓到我作为一个 PM。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I've had the exact same experience. I had to describe what I've done, and it was like 70% mistaken.
turns.zh: 我有完全一样的经历。我得描述我做过什么，它大概 70% 是错的。

turns.speaker: Casey Winters
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there anything you've found value in yet with GPT of any kind in your work, or is it still kind of just poking around and novelty for you?
turns.zh: 到目前为止，你在任何 GPT 里有找到价值的东西吗，还是对你来说还只是捣鼓、新鲜感？

turns.speaker: Casey Winters
turns.en: Yeah. I've had a couple of those things where it's like, "Hey, how do I actually get this weird thing done?" It's been like clear bullet points, take these steps, and I'm like, "Oh, great. This was actually really hard to find on Google." Things like that, I actually quite like it for, so that's where my head goes to more confidently use it. Of course, I'll try it and if it's wrong-
turns.zh: 对。我有几件这样的事，像"嘿，我怎么真把那个怪东西搞定？"它给的像清晰的要点、走这几步，我就想"哦，好。这个在 Google 上其实很难找。"这种事，我其实挺喜欢它，所以那是我更放心用它去的地方。当然，我会试，如果它是错的——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Just throw it away.
turns.zh: 直接扔掉。

turns.speaker: Casey Winters
turns.en: ... I'll learn where it's wrong, so it's low-risk, but it's been right on some of those things and it's like, "Oh, cool. I couldn't figure out how to do that." There was something on Google Docs that I needed to figure out how to do that was kind of fancy. I asked ChatGPT. It told me how to do it, and I was like, "Oh, great."
turns.zh: ……我会学到它哪错，所以低风险，但它在有些事上是对的，就像"哦，酷。我搞不懂怎么弄那个。"Google Docs 上有个我得搞懂怎么弄、有点花哨的东西。我问了 ChatGPT。它告诉我怎么弄，我就想"哦，好。"

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I had a similar experience where I just needed a formula in Google Sheets, and just told it like, "I need this thing," and it just gives me the actual formula.
turns.zh: 我有类似经历，就是我只需要 Google Sheets 里一个公式，告诉它"我要这个东西"，它就直接给我实际公式。

turns.speaker: Casey Winters
turns.en: Yeah, that's so magical when it happens.
turns.zh: 对，发生这种事时太神奇了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. I don't know. I'm not that good with Sheets formulas. Shifting course a little bit, you also wrote this really interesting post on founder intuition versus team expertise. There's a lot to it, and I think it's a really interesting topic because it's this classic discussion that startups have. How much should a founder trust their gut, and how much should it be top-down, "Here's what we should be doing" versus the team, bottom-up, figure out what to build? I'd love to spend a little time here. Maybe just to start broadly, what is this? You came up with a framework of how to think about when founder intuition should overrule, say, team expertise, and how that change over time, so maybe just talk about that.
turns.zh: 对。我不知道。我不太会 Sheets 公式。转个弯，你也写了篇很有意思的帖子，关于创始人直觉 vs 团队专业。里面很多内容，我觉得这话题很有意思，因为它是初创经典的讨论。创始人该多信自己的直觉，该多自上而下——"这是我们要做的"——vs 团队自下而上想出该建什么？我想在这花点时间。也许先从大面说起，这是什么？你搞了个框架想怎么想"什么时候创始人直觉该压过团队专业"，以及这怎么随时间变，所以也许就聊那个。

turns.speaker: Casey Winters
turns.en: Yeah. If founders are lucky/good enough to find product-market fit, they've usually built up all this intuition about their customers, about their product, and their business that are really hard to explain to others and may even be subconscious. When they start to hire people, these people will come in with a lot of excitement, ideas, maybe even really relevant experience, especially senior leaders. I've seen some founders are like, "Cool. I need to let these experts start to own these areas and get out of the geek house." I think that's actually the opposite of what you want, because none of these people know the business as well as you get it. You actually need to direct them until they show you they've really got it and are making better decisions than you would. (00:29:17): This is not a founder example, but I remember when I hired Erika Warren to build out our loyalty program at Grubhub, and she now leads growth at Change.org. After a month or so, she was like, "Dude, you're in all my meetings. I got this." That let me know she was in a different part of the situational leadership framework than I had put her in, so I backed away, and she crushed it from there. (00:29:40): Founders will put a lot of new leaders in that delegate bucket too quickly. It's like, "Ah, they got it. They know more than me," when founders actually know the right answer and should just tell them. This can, of course, change like in the case of Erika. If you hire the right people, they do get smarter than you. You can and you should start delegating. Many founders don't notice the signals where their founder intuition has been usurped by team expertise, or maybe it's just ebbed in effectiveness over time. That, of course, makes sense. Founders have all these different things they're dealing with, and your employees can really dive deep in certain areas. I encourage employees to proactively signal both directions, like, "Hey, I need direction from you." Or, "Hey, I got it from here. Trust me on this one."
turns.zh: 对。如果创始人够幸运/够好，找到了产品市场契合，他们通常已经积累了所有关于客户、产品、业务的直觉，那些很难跟别人解释、甚至可能是潜意识的。当他们开始招人，这些人会带着很多兴奋、想法、甚至很相关的经验进来，尤其是资深领导。我看到一些创始人像"酷。我得让这些专家开始 own 这些领域、从我那张 geek 椅上下来。"我觉得那其实跟你想的相反，因为这些人没一个像你那样懂这业务。你其实得指挥他们，直到他们向你证明他们真懂了、在做比你更好的决定。（00:29:17）这不是创始人的例子，但我记得我在 Grubhub 招 Erika Warren 建我们的忠诚度计划时，她现在在 Change.org 领导增长。大概一个月后，她说"兄弟，你在我所有会里。我搞定了。"那让我知道她在我给她安排的领导情境框架里的位置，跟我以为的不同，所以我就退后了，她从那之后碾压一切。（00:29:40）创始人会把很多新领导太快放进"授权"那个桶。就像"啊，他们搞定了。他们比我懂，"而其实创始人知道正确答案、就该直接告诉他们。这当然能变，像 Erika 那个情况。如果你招对的人，他们确实会变比你聪明。你可以、也应该开始授权。很多创始人没注意到那些信号——他们的创始人直觉被团队专业取代了，或者也许只是随时间有效性退潮了。那当然说得通。创始人有一堆不同的事要处理，而你的员工能真扎进某些领域。我鼓励员工主动双向给信号，像"嘿，我需要你的方向。"或者"嘿，这我来搞定。信我这一次。"

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Interesting. You're saying, as a founder, the heuristic should be if you feel confident about a decision, generally, you should be clear, like, "Hey, I think I know what we need to be doing here," and don't just make people feel better, necessarily, by just saying, "Okay. You tell us what you want to do." Then on the flip side, as an employee at the company, if you feel really confident about something, make it clear to the founder like, "I really think this is the right move." Is there anything more you want to add there?
turns.zh: 有意思。你是说，作为创始人，启发式应该是：如果你对一个决定有信心，总体上你应该清楚，像"嘿，我觉得我知道我们这该做什么，"而不只是为了让别人感觉好，就说"好，你告诉我们你想做什么。"反过来，作为公司里的员工，如果你对某事真有信心，就跟创始人清楚说"我真的觉得这是正确的走法。"还有什么你想补充的吗？

turns.speaker: Casey Winters
turns.en: Yeah. Well, there's obviously the feedback loop of that, of what happens when you do either of those things. Depending on the founder's response to that or the employee's response to that, there's different approaches you can take.
turns.zh: 对。嗯，显然有那个的反馈环，就是当你做这两件事之一时会发生什么。取决于创始人对那个的回应、或员工对那个的回应，有不同的方法你可以采取。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Part of this, you have this cool chart of just over time, the founder expertise becomes less and less relevant. I guess, is that because they just don't spend as much time with the customers because they have other stuff going on or they hire people that are smarter, and then over time, the team expertise goes up?
turns.zh: 这部分，你有个很酷的图，就是随时间，创始人专业变得越来越不相关。我猜，是因为他们就是没花那么多时间跟客户在一起，因为他们有别的事，或者他们招了更聪明的人，然后随时间，团队专业升上去了？

turns.speaker: Casey Winters
turns.en: If you're lucky enough to scale a company, there's just more and more things going on that all will reach the founder in some way, but it means more breadth and less depth on any particular issue, and the reverse is true for people you hire. They're able to get really deep into things that maybe you were really deep into two years ago but you just can't stay deep in anymore. I built this chart on, or I guess I should say table on the different phases of a startup. When you're finding product-market fit, everything goes through the founders. You cannot outsource that. (00:32:08): Then when you start scaling the company because you found product-market fit, it's the first time that founders run into this classic problem of what got you here won't get you there. What got you to product-market fit was iterating on product and doing things that don't scale. Guess what? You found a product that works. Don't do that anymore. Make it scale. Don't come up with new products. You found the one that works. The reason I came up with this framework originally is when I was at Grubhub, we were scaling pretty nicely and fairly organically. (00:32:39): I think Mike and Matt, the founders, had intuited these phases of building a company pretty well, but we acquired a competitor and I saw how that company we acquired operated. Even though they were largely in the same phase as us, they still operated like they were founding the company. Everything was going through the founder. Intuitively, I was like, "Oh, this is why we're acquiring you, and not the other way around." (00:33:09): I think it's really hard for founders to get those signals organically, and I think it's up to us as employees to help. The founders can listen to the signals or not listen to those signals, but that's part of why we're here, but we should also give those signals when we're confident we really get it. Not come in day one being, "I know what your sales strategy should be. You're doing it all wrong." Because chances are, the founders weren't doing it all wrong. They knew something you don't know about yet.
turns.zh: 如果你够幸运把公司规模化，就是有越来越多的事在发生，都会以某种方式到达创始人那里，但那意味着在任何特定问题上更广、更浅，而你招的人正好相反。他们能扎得很深，进那些你两年前也许扎得很深、但现在就是没法再保持深的事。我建了这个图——或者我该说表——关于初创的不同阶段。当你在找产品市场契合时，一切经过创始人。你不能外包那个。（00:32:08）然后当你因为找到 PMF 而开始规模化公司，那是创始人第一次撞上这个经典问题：带你到这的，带不到那。带你到 PMF 的，是在产品上迭代、做那些无法规模化的事。猜怎么着？你找到了一个能用的产品。别再那么干了。让它规模化。别再想出新产品的点子。你找到了那个能用的。我最初搞出这个框架，是因为我在 Grubhub 时，我们规模化得挺好、也挺有机。（00:32:39）我觉得 Mike 和 Matt，那两个创始人，已经挺好凭直觉把握了建公司的这些阶段，但我们收购了一个竞品，我看到我们收购的那家公司怎么运作。即使他们大体跟我们同阶段，他们还是像在创公司一样运作。一切经过创始人。直觉上我就想"哦，这就是为什么是我们收购你，而不是反过来。"（00:33:09）我觉得创始人很难有机地拿到那些信号，我觉得靠我们员工作为帮忙。创始人可以听那些信号、也可以不听，但那是我们在这的部分原因，但我们该在我们有信心真懂的时候也给那些信号。别第一天进来就"我知道你销售策略该是什么。你全做错了。"因为大概率，创始人没全做错。他们知道一些你还不知道的东西。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What is it that you think made it such that you won and they didn't? Is it because they didn't invest, they didn't shift to scaling and delegating to their employees as much as the founder just telling everyone to do it?
turns.zh: 你觉得是什么让你赢了、他们没赢？是因为他们没投、没像创始人那样转到规模化、授权给员工，而是创始人就告诉所有人去做？

turns.speaker: Casey Winters
turns.en: Correct, right. Everything was not moving as quickly because everything had to go through the same person to get done. It just allowed them to not launch as many markets, not sign up as many restaurants, to not figure out as many growth channels, yeah, as we had done.
turns.zh: 对，对。一切都动得没那么快，因为一切得经过同一个人才能做完。那只是让他们没法 launch 那么多市场、签不到那么多餐厅、搞不出那么多增长渠道，对，不像我们做的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Got it. They just bottlenecked themselves and they weren't able to move as fast because the founder thought they needed to make these decisions, and they were still the ones that knew everything.
turns.zh: 懂了。他们就是自己卡住了自己，没法动那么快，因为创始人觉得他们需要做这些决定，而他们还是那个什么都知道的人。

turns.speaker: Casey Winters
turns.en: Yep.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That makes me think about most companies. Maybe not most, but many founders just believe they have the answers. They are confident they know what to do, and it's rare they get to a place of like, "Nah, I actually don't."
turns.zh: 这让我想到大多数公司。也许不是大多数，但很多创始人就是相信他们有答案。他们有信心知道该做什么，很少到那种"不，其实我不知道"的地方。

turns.speaker: Casey Winters
turns.en: Well, I would say no one gets to it super intuitively.
turns.zh: 嗯，我会说没人能超直觉地到达那。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Any advice for either as a employee at a company with a founder like that or leader, of just how to push back and help the founder understand, "Maybe you should let go and trust people to make decisions"?
turns.zh: 对作为那样一个创始人的公司里的员工或领导，有什么建议，就怎么推回、帮创始人理解"也许你该放手、信别人去做决定"？

turns.speaker: Casey Winters
turns.en: I think the first thing is you have to understand that it's their company, not yours, and the founders have impossible jobs. They're not going to scale perfectly with the needs of the company. It's just something's going to be off. It may be because there's a whole lot of hubris by being the one of a thousand startups that made it, or they just have personal styles, but they can run the company any way they want. (00:35:08): I think it's sometimes surprising when founders actually want to run things suboptimally. I think we've seen examples where founders just want to build cool shit versus focusing on what customers want, or they're too obsessed with the design. They're always rebranding, redesigning things in ways that confuse customers. Of course, that's going to happen and those are some of the worst cases. I think if you do state your point, you've actually built up the expertise, you're confident and you are refuted for whatever reasons, you have to find ways to be contrarian and prove you're right. (00:35:43): Different founders have different forms of feedback they listen to. It might be talking to other CEOs, or other operators, or trusted advisors, certain customers. Some might be very data-oriented, so you just run the experiment and ask for forgiveness after you proved it works, whatever. Everyone's got a different thing they respond to. You try to figure out what actually influences the CEO and build that case, whether it's through an experiment, the right customer intro, the right external advisor. If they rebuke that as well, then you got to disagree and commit, or find a new company to join, or start your own. Like I said, it's their company. They can make the call. (00:36:25): I remember when I joined Pinterest, I was just coming off 100X increase in user growth from Grubhub. I was ready to drive the same sort of impact at Pinterest, but no one knew who I was. I didn't come from Facebook or Google like most of the other people, or Pinterest. No one gave a shit about Chicago startups at the time, so when they didn't trust my proposals, I just went and talked to the heads of growth at all the startups they did respect. I talked to Dropbox, I talked to Facebook. When they said all the same things I was saying but I said that they said it, not me, that was, sadly, more convincing. I didn't care because I still got what I wanted out of it, which is to do the right thing to grow the company.
turns.zh: 我觉得第一件事是，你得明白那是他们的公司，不是你的，而创始人的工作是不可能完成的。他们不会完美地跟上公司需求地规模化。就是会有东西偏掉。也许是因为作为千分之一活下来的初创的创始人有海量傲慢，或者只是他们个人风格，但他们可以用任何他们想要的方式运营公司。（00:35:08）我觉得有时创始人大概想以次优的方式运营，挺让人意外的。我们看到过例子，创始人就是想建很酷的 shit，而不是聚焦客户想要什么，或者他们对设计太痴迷。他们总在重塑品牌、重做设计，方式把客户搞晕。当然，那会发生，而那些是一些最糟的情况。我觉得如果你真陈述了你的点、你真的建起了专业、你有信心、然后你因为无论什么原因被驳回，你得找到方式去唱反调、证明你是对的。（00:35:43）不同创始人听不同的反馈形式。可能是跟其他 CEO、其他操盘手、信任的顾问、某些客户聊。有些可能非常数据导向，所以你直接跑实验、在证明它有效之后再求原谅，随便。每个人都有不同的东西能打动他们。你试着弄清什么真能影响 CEO、建那个案子，无论是通过实验、对的客户引荐、对的外部顾问。如果他们连那个也驳回，那你就得"不同意但执行"，或者找家新公司加入，或者自己创。就像我说的，那是他们的公司。他们能做决定。（00:36:25）我记得我加入 Pinterest 时，刚从 Grubhub 带来 100 倍的用户增长。我准备好在 Pinterest 驱动同样的影响，但没人知道我是谁。我不像大多数人那样来自 Facebook 或 Google，或 Pinterest。当时没人在乎芝加哥的初创。所以当他们不信任我的提案，我就去跟所有他们尊重的初创的增长负责人聊。我聊了 Dropbox，我聊了 Facebook。当他们说出跟我说的完全一样的话、但我说是他们说的、不是我，那——可悲地——更有说服力。我不在乎，因为我还是拿到了我想要的结果，也就是做对的事去增长公司。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Now you're one of those people that people go to. If Casey says it, it's probably the right way to do it.
turns.zh: 现在你是那些人们会去请教的人之一了。如果 Casey 说了，那大概是做这事的正确方式。

turns.speaker: Casey Winters
turns.en: Whether I'm correct or not, it is a role I sometimes play in the ecosystem, I will admit.
turns.zh: 无论我对不对，我承认，这是我有时在这个生态里扮演的角色。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there an example where you were convinced something was the right way to go and the founder at one of the companies you worked at had a different opinion and they had ended up being right.
turns.zh: 有没有个例子，是你确信某条路是对的、而你待过的某家公司的创始人有不同意见、最后他们是对的？

turns.speaker: Casey Winters
turns.en: When I was at Grubhub, one of the ideas one of the founders came up with was to build an app for delivery drivers. At the time, restaurants had their own delivery drivers. They did not work for us. We wanted to build an app for the delivery drivers so you could see where the food was along the way, so you could know if it's five minutes away, whatever. Domino's was the first to have done this at the time, and we thought that would make a bunch of sense. (00:37:48): I was just like, "How am I supposed to convince the delivery driver, who doesn't have a relationship with us, to download the app from Grubhub, to actually turn it on, to create anxiety for the consumer of they maybe didn't take the right turn or, whatever?" I was like, "I don't think this makes sense. No one's going to use it," and Mike and Matt overruled me and pushed us to do it. (00:38:10): In the long run, it ended up being quite necessary because of the innovations around DoorDash, and Postmates, and later, Uber Eats having their own delivery network and us needing to counter that. That's, of course, a key piece of technology that needs to have parity with those new services. That was an area where perhaps, they were thinking a little bit more longer term than I was, and I was not able to get where they were going on the longer-term time horizon of how this would be actually ultimately adopted and useful.
turns.zh: 我在 Grubhub 时，有个创始人想出的点子之一是给外卖司机建个 app。当时，餐厅有自己的外卖司机。他们不为我们工作。我们想给外卖司机建个 app，这样你能看到食物一路到哪了，能知道是不是还有五分钟到，随便。Domino's 当时是第一个这么做的，我们觉得那会很有道理。（00:37:48）我就想"我要怎么说服那个跟我们没关系的外卖司机，去下载 Grubhub 的 app、真的打开它、给消费者制造焦虑——比如他可能拐错弯了，随便？"我就想"我觉得这没道理。没人会用它，"然后 Mike 和 Matt 推翻了我、推着我们去做。（00:38:10）长远看，它最后变得相当必要，因为 DoorDash、Postmates、后来 Uber Eats 围绕自己的配送网络搞的创新，而我们需要对抗那个。那当然是需要跟那些新服务平起平坐的关键技术。那是个他们也许比我想得更长远的地方，而我没能到他们去的那个长远时间线上——关于这东西最终会怎么被采用、变得有用。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This is an awesome segue to the next area, but real quick, how did they get drivers to start using this app? Was there anything really clever they did?
turns.zh: 这很好地过渡到下一个领域，但快问一句，他们怎么让司机开始用这个 app 的？他们做了什么真的聪明的事吗？

turns.speaker: Casey Winters
turns.en: I think it was fairly low adoption for a while, and leveraging basically restaurant authority. If we're able to push on our restaurant customers effectively to say like, "Hey, if you use this, it'll get you more orders. We'll get you prominence in the UI," things like that to then push down to their direct relationships with the drivers to get them to adopt.
turns.zh: 我觉得它有一阵子采用率相当低，基本是借餐厅的权威。如果我们能有效地推我们的餐厅客户，说"嘿，如果你用这个，它会给你更多订单。我们会在 UI 里给你突出位置，"之类，再往下推到他们跟司机的直接关系上，让他们采用。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. This episode is brought to you by Ahrefs. You probably know Ahrefs as one of the leading all-in-one SEO tools used by companies like Facebook, Uber, Shopify, LinkedIn, Pinterest, and thousands more, but Ahrefs is not just for big companies. With their new Ahrefs webmaster tools, you can optimize your personal website like a professional for free. You can scan your website for over a hundred common SEO issues that might be hurting your performance in search engines, plus get advice on how to fix those errors. (00:39:39): You can have it automatically browse your website's internal and external links and get actionable insights from your backlink profiles, and you can learn what keywords your website ranks for and see how you stack up against your competitors. Visit ahrefs.com/awt and start improving your website's visibility. That's ahrefs.com/awt. (00:40:00): Okay. Shifting to our last topic that I was excited to chat about is around network effects, and marketplaces, and SaaS, and how those things connect. I feel like you have the clearest way of thinking about and explaining network effects, so maybe just to start, can you just simply explain what is a network effect and then the different types of network effects that exist?
turns.zh: 太棒了。本期节目由 Ahrefs 赞助。你大概知道 Ahrefs 是领先的万能 SEO 工具之一，被 Facebook、Uber、Shopify、LinkedIn、Pinterest 等上千家公司使用，但 Ahrefs 不只是给大公司。用他们新的 Ahrefs webmaster 工具，你可以免费像专业人士一样优化你的个人网站。你可以扫描你网站一百多个常见的 SEO 问题——那些可能在伤害你在搜索引擎表现的问题——外加拿到怎么修这些错误的建议。（00:39:39）它能自动浏览你网站的内外链，从你的反向链接画像拿到可执行的洞察，你还能学到你的网站排哪些关键词、看你怎么跟竞争对手比。去 ahrefs.com/awt，开始提升你网站的可见性。就是 ahrefs.com/awt。（00:40:00）好。转到我们最后一个我 excited 想聊的话题，关于网络效应、市场、SaaS，以及这些东西怎么连起来。我觉得你对网络效应有最清晰的理解和解释方式，所以也许先从简单开始，你能简单解释什么是网络效应、然后有哪些不同类型的网络效应吗？

turns.speaker: Casey Winters
turns.en: Yeah. No pressure after you say that. Yeah, so at it's core, a network effect is when a product or a business gets better with more users or customers using it. There's three types that I tend to focus on. The first and probably the most well-known is called direct network effects. That's when every additional user makes the product better for all the existing users. When someone joins WhatsApp, other people can talk to them that wouldn't be able to talk to them before, and that makes WhatsApp valuable, more valuable for everyone. (00:40:55): Then there are cross-side network effects where there's two distinct types of users, and adding an additional user on one side of the network makes it more valuable for all the types of users on the other side of the network and vice-versa. When a restaurant joins Grubhub, it creates more selection for users to order food, and when more users start ordering more food, Grubhub becomes more attractive for restaurants to join so they can make more money from delivery orders. (00:41:21): The last network effect I focus on is data network effects. That's when the quality or cost of something improves as more data is collected through the product. When you say content to Pinterest, to a board, it gives Pinterest signal on the quality of that content, its relevance to other pieces of content, since they're shared to the same board, and more signal on your preferences. This allows Pinterest to better recommend more content to you as well as to other people who look like you and share similar interests. (00:41:55): One thing that's tricky about these network effects is most people talk about network effects in the context of social network, not marketplaces or SaaS like my background. The thing that's really tricky in understanding social networks is they're traditionally described as these direct network effect businesses, but all of them have to become either cross-side and/or data and network effect businesses over time. The only companies that stay direct network effect businesses are these pure communication tools like Messenger, iMessage, WhatsApp. There isn't a clear path to make money with those, but you want to sell ads, you're becoming a cross-side network effect business. Also, creators verse consumers creates a cross-side network effect business. If you want to get better at personalization, guess what? You're recommending content by leveraging data network effects.
turns.zh: 对。你这么说完就没压力了哈。对，所以核心是，网络效应是当一款产品或生意随着更多用户或客户使用它而变得更好。我一般聚焦三种。第一种、可能最知名的，叫直接网络效应。那是每个新增用户让产品对所有现存用户更好。有人加入 WhatsApp，别人就能跟他们聊，而以前聊不了，那让 WhatsApp 更有价值，对所有人更有价值。（00:40:55）然后有跨边网络效应，那里有两类不同的用户，在一边加一个用户，让网络另一边的所有用户更有价值，反之亦然。一个餐厅加入 Grubhub，给用户创造了更多选择去点餐；而当更多用户开始点更多餐，Grubhub 对餐厅变得更有吸引力，这样他们能从配送订单赚更多钱。（00:41:21）我聚焦的最后一个网络效应是数据网络效应。那是当通过产品收集更多数据，某东西的质量或成本改善。当你把内容存到 Pinterest、存到一个画板，它给 Pinterest 那个内容质量的信号、它跟其他内容的关联——因为它们被分享到同一个画板——以及更多关于你偏好的信号。这让 Pinterest 更好地给你、以及给跟你像、有相似兴趣的人推荐更多内容。（00:41:55）这些网络效应里一件棘手的事是，大多数人谈网络效应是在社交网络的语境里，而不是市场或 SaaS——我的背景。理解社交网络真正棘手的是，它们传统上被描述为这些直接网络效应的生意，但所有社交网络随时间都必须变成跨边和/或数据网络效应的生意。唯一保持直接网络效应生意的，是这些纯沟通工具，像 Messenger、iMessage、WhatsApp。用那些赚钱没有明确路径，但你想卖广告，你就变成跨边网络效应生意。还有，创作者 vs 消费者，创造了跨边网络效应生意。如果你想在个性化上更好，猜怎么着？你在用数据网络效应推荐内容。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that. You nailed it. I imagine marketplace founders listening to this may be wondering, "Hey, can I add on these additional network effects? Can I evolve towards one of these?" What you're saying is not only can you, you need to, eventually.
turns.zh: 我爱这个。你说到位了。我想象市场创始人在听这个，也许在想"嘿，我能加上这些额外的网络效应吗？我能演进到其中一个吗？"你说的不仅是能，你是最终必须。

turns.speaker: Casey Winters
turns.en: I agree. I think they're a great form of defensibility, first off. Do they make sense for every business? No, but in a lot of cases, in order for you to evolve properly and continue to grow, they can become a necessity.
turns.zh: 我同意。我觉得它们首先是很棒的一种防御力。它们对每门生意都有意义吗？不，但在很多情况下，为了你恰当地演进、持续增长，它们能变成一种必需。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Are there any other examples of marketplace companies that come to mind that did a great job evolving or adding one of these network effects or are just interesting?
turns.zh: 有没有其他市场公司的例子浮现在你脑海，做得很好地演进或加了一个网络效应、或者就是有意思的？

turns.speaker: Casey Winters
turns.en: Let's take some inventory. I think Zillow is really interesting in that a real estate listing site is not particularly an interesting product, but the ability of saying, very rarely do both sides of this network, people who are buying homes and selling homes need to connect, but I can find a way for the brand to connect with both of them by giving real time pricing information on the value of homes, and that creates a much stickier product for both sides. I think that was a pretty genuine innovation that other people have tried and rarely been as successful with. That's one that definitely sticks with me off the top of my head.
turns.zh: 我们盘一下。我觉得 Zillow 真的有意思，因为房产挂牌网站不是个特别有意思的产品，但说"这个网络两边——买房的人和卖房的人——很少需要连接"的能力，而我找到一种方式让品牌通过给房屋价值的实时定价信息，连接两边，那给两边都创造了黏得多的产品。我觉得那是相当真诚的创新，别人试过、很少像它那么成功。那是我想到就记得的一个。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Great. We've been talking about Grubhub a lot. Grubhub had some pretty strong network effects, in large part, thanks to the work you did. One of the benefits of network effects is it creates a barrier to entry. It's hard to replicate and compete with a company where they already have all this network effect, but famously, Grubhub got disrupted by DoorDash and Uber Eats. Maybe you can talk about how that happened and why that happened. It'd be cool to hear just like, what do you think they could have done differently and what happened where their network effect got eaten for lunch? Pun intended.
turns.zh: 好。我们一直在聊 Grubhub。Grubhub 有相当强的网络效应，很大程度上，多亏了你做的事。网络效应的一个好处是它创造了进入壁垒。已经有一堆网络效应的公司，很难复制、很难与之竞争，但出了名的，Grubhub 被 DoorDash 和 Uber Eats 颠覆了。也许你能讲讲那怎么发生的、为什么发生。听到"你觉得他们本可以做什么不同"、以及他们的网络效应怎么被抢了饭碗，会很酷。双关无意。

turns.speaker: Casey Winters
turns.en: Sure. It's a great question. I think people do mistake any form of network effect as this perfect form of defensibility. They're the best form of defensibility, but that doesn't mean they're immune to disruption. I think the main way this happens with cross-side network effects that we typically talk about for marketplaces is when a disruptor dramatically expands selection. I want to be clear, I left Grubhub at the end of 2013 before said lunch was eaten, so what I'm communicating is more like public knowledge of watching these amazing companies compete, rather than being inside the fire at the time.
turns.zh: 当然。好问题。我觉得人们确实把任何形态的网络效应当成这种完美的防御形式。它们是最好的防御形式，但那不意味着它们对颠覆免疫。我觉得这发生的主要方式——我们一般对市场谈的跨边网络效应——是当颠覆者戏剧性地扩大选择。我想说清楚，我在 2013 年底离开 Grubhub，在那顿饭被吃之前，所以我沟通的更多是看着这些惊人公司竞争的公开知识，而不是当时在火里。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Great.
turns.zh: 好。

turns.speaker: Casey Winters
turns.en: But one important thing to remember is Grubhub was an asset-light marketplace model. Restaurants did their own delivery through their own delivery drivers that they hired. I wrote this post for Andreessen Horowitz a few years ago about supply strategies and marketplaces, so in that you really need to be comprehensive or have exclusive inventory, and Grubhub strived to be comprehensive. We'd show every restaurant that delivered to you, even if we didn't work with them directly for online ordering. What happened about a year before I left Grubhub was that these competitors started to raise their seed rounds or series As to build delivery networks. (00:45:51): Postmates and DoorDash were the first two that rose to prominence. Uber Eats would come later, but they actually started with a pretty different business model, and this is an extremely different business. You're hiring drivers, you're managing logistics. We call this a heavily managed marketplace model, as you are now facilitating the transaction versus just connecting buyers and sellers and taking payments like Grubhub did. (00:46:18): On the one hand, you have Grubhub, this extremely high-margin business, and these businesses coming up are actually negative-margin businesses. At least they were for a long time. In 2013, Grubhub acquired Seamless, its closest competitor at the time. Seamless still had a lead on Grubhub in New York, partially because it had this corporate program where law firms, and banks, and consultants got lunch stipends you had to redeem by ordering the food through Seamless. Grubhub operated in these dense cities and suburbs like in New York because those were really places that had restaurants that had delivery. (00:46:58): DoorDash, when it started, operated in less dense suburbs and worked with restaurants that had never done delivery before, and they would provide the delivery drivers themselves. This allowed DoorDash to grow without much competition in the early days. These companies also took some real gambles. One of the things they did is they delivered from restaurants they didn't have an agreement with, and that caused controversy and lawsuits. What it meant is when these companies did launch in the cities to go after Grubhub, it felt like DoorDash, and Postmates, and Uber had dramatically larger selection of restaurants to choose from, and Grubhub was definitely no longer near comprehensive. (00:47:40): Back when we talked about cross-side network effects, the more selection of restaurants, the more attractive it is to users and vice-versa. At that point, Grubhub's put in a very peculiar position. It had gone public after raising $80 million in venture capital and raising a $100 million in an IPO, telling investors it's an extremely profitable, high-growth, asset-light marketplace, but now it's got disruption pressure from operationally intensive negative-margin delivery services that were raising $100 million every six months from the private markets. (00:48:14): What Grubhub assumed is that these businesses were just structurally unprofitable, and that VCs would stop subsidizing them eventually. Of course, that didn't happen. They kept raising more money. DoorDash eventually raised multiple billions of dollars in this market. Part of what they used that money for was to lock up agreements with national chains, which Grubhub never worked with. It was always like the local mom and pops, and promotions and discounts on the demand side. All of this is happening, and then the pandemic hits, and all of those negative margins turned positive for DoorDash for the first time, if I understand things correctly. (00:48:53): On top of that, all this corporate ordering that we got from Seamless no longer mattered because no one goes to the office anymore, so this gambit really paid off and DoorDash just took the market. Grubhub then tried to copy the approaches of DoorDash and Postmates. They wrote this famous letter saying that they still thought the approaches were stupid, but their hand was forced, which is kind of funny to read in retrospect. A lot of armchair thinkers are like, "How could Grubhub have been so stupid to let DoorDash take the market that they built?" (00:49:24): Look, I'll admit Grubhub made some mistakes, but I think it would have been extremely hard for Grubhub to come out on top here. Let's say in 2014 after you IPO, you do actually think what DoorDash, Postmates, and Uber are doing are smart. What do you do? Go to investors that you promised high growth and high profits and say you need to raise more money in debt to compete with negative-margin upstarts in a way that will destroy all that potential profit you mentioned? The stock would drop 90%. A lot of your employees would leave because their stock is now worthless. On top of that, building a delivery network is a heavy operations play that matches none of your core competencies, so to me, that feels like a death sentence. (00:50:10): I think the only play here was to buy DoorDash as early as possible, and let DoorDash and their operationally-heavy culture eat Grubhub from the inside out. I think Grubhub probably could have acquired them multiple times. For whatever reason, it never happened. It would have seemed pretty risky had Grubhub done that. Investors probably would have hated it, but it would have been their Netflix moment, where Netflix bet it all on streaming and they bet right. This is all incredibly easy to say in hindsight. (00:50:43): I think what I've learned now that I'm more senior in my career is during existential threats, it's like when Nassim Taleb says, "The only rational reaction is overreaction." Unless you have a real viable reason to assume otherwise, you got to assume the disruptor is right and base your strategy on them playing an optimal game. Whereas, I think Grubhub assumed the disruptor was wrong and that it would all play out eventually in their favor, and it clearly didn't.
turns.zh: 但一件重要的事要记住：Grubhub 是个轻资产市场模型。餐厅用他们自己雇的外卖司机做自己的配送。几年前我给 Andreessen Horowitz 写了篇关于市场与供给策略的帖子，所以在那里面你真的需要全面、或者有独家库存，而 Grubhub 力求全面。我们会显示每个给你配送的餐厅，即使我们没跟他们直接合作做在线点单。大概在我离开 Grubhub 前一年，这些竞品开始融种子轮或 A 轮，去建配送网络。（00:45:51）Postmates 和 DoorDash 是最先冒头的两个。Uber Eats 后来才来，但他们其实从一个相当不同的商业模式起步，而且这是个极不同的生意。你在雇司机、管物流。我们叫这个重管理市场模型，因为你现在是在促成交易，而不是像 Grubhub 那样只是连接买卖两边、收付款。（00:46:18）一方面，你有 Grubhub，这个极高利润率的生意，而这些起来的公司是其实是负利润率的生意。至少它们长期是。2013 年，Grubhub 收购了 Seamless，当时最接近的竞品。Seamless 在纽约还领先 Grubhub，部分因为有个企业项目——律所、银行、咨询公司拿午餐补贴，必须通过 Seamless 点餐才能兑换。Grubhub 在这些密集城市和郊区像纽约运营，因为那些真有做配送的餐厅。（00:46:58）DoorDash 起步时，在没那么密集的郊区运营，跟从没做过配送的餐厅合作，他们自己提供外卖司机。这让 DoorDash 在早期没什么竞争就能增长。这些公司也下了些真赌注。他们做的一件事是，从他们没协议的餐厅配送，那引发了争议和诉讼。那意味着当这些公司确实在城里 launch、去抢 Grubhub 时，感觉上 DoorDash、Postmates、Uber 有戏剧性更大的餐厅选择，而 Grubhub 绝对不再接近全面了。（00:47:40）回到我们谈跨边网络效应，餐厅选择越多，对用户越有吸引力，反之亦然。在那时，Grubhub 处在一个很奇特的位置。它在融了 8000 万风险投资、又 IPO 融了 1 亿之后上市了，告诉投资人这是个极高利润、高增长、轻资产的市场，但现在它受到来自运营密集、负利润配送服务的颠覆压力——那些服务每六个月从私募市场融 1 亿。（00:48:14）Grubhub 假设的是这些生意结构上就是亏的，而 VC 最终会停止补贴它们。当然，那没发生。他们持续融更多钱。DoorDash 最终在这个市场融了几十亿。他们用那钱的一部分，去锁定跟全国连锁的协议——Grubhub 从没合作过。它一直是本地夫妻店，加上需求侧的促销和折扣。这一切都在发生，然后疫情来了，所有这些负利润第一次转成正——如果我理解得对。（00:48:53）除此之外，我们从 Seamless 拿到的所有企业订单不再重要了，因为没人去办公室了，所以这个赌注真的 payoff 了，DoorDash 就直接拿下了市场。Grubhub 然后试图抄 DoorDash 和 Postmates 的做法。他们写了那封著名的信，说他们还是觉得那些做法蠢，但他们的手被逼了，回头看挺好笑的。很多纸上谈兵的人像"Grubhub 怎么蠢到让 DoorDash 拿走他们建起的市场？"（00:49:24）看，我承认 Grubhub 犯了些错，但我觉得 Grubhub 要在这里脱颖而出会极难。假设 2014 年你 IPO 后，你真觉得 DoorDash、Postmates、Uber 做的聪明。你怎么做？去你承诺了高增长高利润的投资人那，说你需要融更多债去跟负利润的新贵竞争、那种会摧毁你提的所有潜在利润的方式？股票会跌 90%。你很多员工会走，因为他们的股票现在一文不值。除此之外，建配送网络是个重运营玩法，跟你任何核心能力都不匹配，所以对我而言那像死刑。（00:50:10）我觉得这里唯一的打法是尽可能早地买下 DoorDash，让 DoorDash 和他们重运营的文化从内到外吃掉 Grubhub。我觉得 Grubhub 大概能多次收购他们。无论什么原因，没发生。如果 Grubhub 那么做了会显得相当冒险。投资人可能恨死，但那会是他们的 Netflix 时刻——Netflix 把一切押在流媒体上、押对了。这都是事后说极其容易。（00:50:43）我觉得我现在职业生涯更资深学到的：在生存威胁期间，就像 Nassim Taleb 说的"唯一理性的反应就是过度反应。"除非你有真正可行的理由假设相反，你得假设颠覆者是对的、把你的战略建立在他们玩最优游戏上。而我觉得 Grubhub 假设颠覆者是错的、一切最终会对他们有利，而显然没有。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow. I have never heard that full story. That was amazing. Thank you for getting in so much detail there.
turns.zh: 哇。我从没听过那个完整故事。太精彩了。感谢你讲那么细。

turns.speaker: Casey Winters
turns.en: I don't know how much of it is right, but-
turns.zh: 我不知道多少是对的，但——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It seems right, from the outside. It's interesting that it's like a version of innovator's dilemma. Usually, innovator's dilemma is people come and do something cheaper at the low end of the market. In this case, it was more they were doing something that they didn't believe would scale. It was just much more inefficient-
turns.zh: 从外面看是对的。有意思的是它像创新者窘境的一个版本。通常，创新者窘境是别人来、在市场低端做更便宜的东西。在这个案例，更多是他们在做他们认为无法规模化的东西。只是效率低得多——

turns.speaker: Casey Winters
turns.en: Correct.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: ... even though it was a better experience. Is that innovator's dilemma, or is that some other version of innovator's dilemma? Because to your point, they couldn't almost go after it.
turns.zh: ……即使它是更好的体验。那是创新者窘境吗，还是创新者窘境的某个别的版本？因为按你的点，他们几乎没法去追它。

turns.speaker: Casey Winters
turns.en: I think it is in spirit, for sure.
turns.zh: 我觉得在精神上，绝对是。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The takeaway there that you've learned is don't underestimate someone that's trying to do something that's going to eat your lunch eventually, even though it feels like a terrible business model.
turns.zh: 你学到的结论是：别低估那个试图做最终会抢你饭碗的事的人，即使它感觉像个糟透的商业模式。

turns.speaker: Casey Winters
turns.en: Right. If the market's rewarding it, the market will probably find a way to make it profitable. It's essentially, when everyone's find a more efficient network effect for demand on the marketplace side, you probably need to copy that as soon as possible, and if you can't copy it, own it, buy it. I think we've seen this a few times. Rover and Wag was another interesting example of this, where they found a more frequent use case that fit the same supply and demand, and Rover just copied it as soon as possible. That ended up working out for them in a way that it didn't as much for Grubhub.
turns.zh: 对。如果市场在奖励它，市场大概会找到让它盈利的方式。本质上，当每个人都在市场侧找到更高效的网络效应，你可能得尽快抄它，如果抄不了，就拥有它、买它。我觉得我们见过几次这个。Rover 和 Wag 是另一个有意思的例子，他们找到了一个更高频的用例，契合同样的供给和需求，而 Rover 尽快抄了它。那对他们管用的程度，跟对 Grubhub 不一样。（00:53:40）

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I just did a talk recently on marketplace growth strategy, and someone asked me a really interesting question. "If you were trying to go up against a DoorDash or an Uber today, what would you do?" My answer is just like, money was so freely available at that point that they were able to ... A lot of this was spend. They had so much money raised. You said they were raising $100 million every six months. Is it even possible in today's climate, where you can't actually raise that much money, to have any sort of chance to beat a DoorDash or an Uber?
turns.zh: 我最近刚做了个关于市场增长策略的演讲，有人问了我个很有意思的问题。"如果你想今天去对抗一个 DoorDash 或 Uber，你会做什么？"我的答案大概是，当时钱那么自由可得，他们能……很多这是花钱。他们融了那么多钱。你说他们每六个月融 1 亿。在今天的气候下，你其实融不到那么多钱，还有任何机会打败 DoorDash 或 Uber 吗？

turns.speaker: Casey Winters
turns.en: Yeah, clearly, they took advantage of the zero interest rate environments that we talked about earlier. That is not a replicable strategy in 2023. Any approach to compete with them has to be competing on a very different angle because, yeah, they can spend you into the dust. We'll see if anyone's able to build a way that creates new supply in market. I think you and I have seen a couple of earlier stage examples of that. We'll see if any of them scale, or something that feels cheaper or more fun on the demand side. That would be another way to potentially disrupt things. (00:53:40): I think another thing that was working pretty well before the pandemic in building disrupters was focusing on the pickup use case, which DoorDash cannot do as easily. They've tried, but their whole value prop is the delivery network, which you don't need for pickup. Of course, the pandemic put a lot of those startups grinding to a halt as well. There's always angles, but you're going to need to be incredibly clever because just attacking with a war chest is not really going to work.
turns.zh: 对。显然，他们利用了我们早先聊的零利率环境。那在 2023 年不是个可复制的战略。任何跟他们竞争的方法，必须在一个非常不同的角度竞争，因为，对，他们能把你花钱花到尘埃里。我们看会不会有人能建出一种创造市场新供给的方式。我觉得你我也见过几个更早阶段的例子。我们看它们会不会有哪个规模化，或者在需求侧感觉更便宜或更fun 的东西。那会是另一个潜在颠覆的方式。（00:53:40）我觉得疫情前在颠覆者身上管用的另一件事，是聚焦自取（pickup）用例，DoorDash 没那么容易做。他们试过，但他们的整个价值主张是配送网络，而自取不需要那个。当然，疫情让很多那些初创也戛然而止。总会有角度，但你得极其聪明，因为光用钱库攻击真的不会管用。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. I noticed a lot of startups launching that are trying to do white label delivery for restaurants so they don't have to rely on DoorDash, but maybe that's a wedge to get in, and eventually they do the DoorDash sort of thing.
turns.zh: 对。我注意到很多 launch 的初创，试图给餐厅做白标配送，这样他们不依赖 DoorDash，但也许那是切入的楔子，最终他们做 DoorDash 那种事。

turns.speaker: Casey Winters
turns.en: Yeah, and I would say I'm pretty skeptical of those because they're just not really building the network effects on the demand side. They're just more like SaaS businesses. I think those struggle to be multi-$100 million in revenue businesses because the take rate is typically like a third or a fourth of what a DoorDash can charge.
turns.zh: 对，我会说我对那些相当怀疑，因为他们就是没真在需求侧建起网络效应。他们更像 SaaS 生意。我觉得那些挣扎着成为数亿美元营收的生意，因为抽成率通常只有 DoorDash 能收的三分之一或四分之一。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Perfect segue to my next question, and I only have a couple more. There's this concept and I think pull from marketplace founders to add a SaaS tool, eventually, and have both business models. Then there's often the reverse, where a SaaS company wants to add a marketplace. I know this question is something you get a lot, and so just a question for you. Does this work? Are there examples where they've added this additional way of making money? Which direction do you find is most often successful and not successful?
turns.zh: 完美过渡到我的下一个问题，而且我就剩几个了。有个概念，我觉得是从市场创始人那拿来的——最终加一个 SaaS 工具、然后有两个商业模式。然后常有反向，一个 SaaS 公司想加一个市场。我知道这个问题你常被问到，所以就问你。这管用吗？有没有他们加了这种额外赚钱方式的例子？你发现哪个方向最常成功、哪个不成功？

turns.speaker: Casey Winters
turns.en: The canonical example that a lot of these founders use is OpenTable. That always felt really unfulfilling to me because it's very old at this point. Probably the younger people listening to the podcast are like, "What's OpenTable?" I think that business has incredibly underperformed the market it operated in. It had a good exit. It sold for $2.6 billion, I think, to Booking.com, but Booking subsequently wrote that value down below a billion, so that's not really the outcome I think we're looking for, traditionally, in marketplaces.
turns.zh: 很多这些创始人用的典范例子是 OpenTable。那一直让我觉得真没满足感，因为它现在很老了。大概听这播客的年轻人像"OpenTable 是什么？"我觉得那生意在它所在的市场的表现，低得惊人。它有个好退出。它卖给了 Booking.com，我记得是 26 亿，但 Booking 随后把那个价值减记到 10 亿以下，所以那不是我们通常对市场期待的结果。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Maybe explain what it was initially, the SaaS tool versus a financial marketplace.
turns.zh: 也许解释一下它最初是什么，SaaS 工具 vs 金融性质的市场。

turns.speaker: Casey Winters
turns.en: Oh, sure. OpenTable promised both a SaaS tool that would help you understand what tables are open and where to seat people, so for the host in the front of the house in a restaurant, but also bring in additional reservations to fill up your restaurant. Because I think what people misunderstand about restaurants is they're, "Oh, these restaurants are these incredibly low-margin businesses." It's like, yeah, they are because they're paying the rent no matter what. (00:56:14): Once you're already paying the rent no matter what happens, you're incentivized to pump as much food out the kitchen and to get as many people seated in-house as possible. People would say like, "Oh, Grubhub and DoorDash are charging too much." It's like, no, delivery orders and catering orders are basically pure margin to restaurants. The chefs are already there. The rent is already being paid. "The more things we pump out of the kitchen, the more money we make," which is why restaurants are willing to pay higher fees. These restaurants are not stupid. They're not being misinformed. OpenTable, well before there were any delivery startups, was like, "We're going to fill up your tables, and we're going to give you software that helps you manage your tables most effectively to make the most profit."
turns.zh: 哦，当然。OpenTable 承诺了两样：一个 SaaS 工具，帮你理解哪些桌空着、该把人安排坐哪——给餐厅前厅那个领位的人用——但也带进额外的预订去填满你的餐厅。因为我觉得人们对餐厅的误解是"哦，这些餐厅是极低利润生意。"就像，对，它们是，因为他们不管怎样都付租金。（00:56:14）一旦你不管发生什么都已在付租金，你就有动力从厨房多泵出食物、尽可能多让人坐进来。人们会说"哦，Grubhub 和 DoorDash 收太多。"就像，不，配送订单和宴席订单对餐厅基本是纯利润。厨师都已经在那了。租金已经付了。"我们从厨房泵出越多，我们赚越多，"这就是为什么餐厅愿意付更高费用。这些餐厅不蠢。他们没被误导。OpenTable，远在任何配送初创之前，就像"我们要填满你的桌，我们要给你软件帮你最有效管理你的桌、赚最多利润。"

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Got it. Okay, great. If you've got-
turns.zh: 懂了。好，棒。如果你有——

turns.speaker: Casey Winters
turns.en: That's OpenTable.
