Look, this is definitely the strategy we are working on with Eventbrite, where we started with something that was more SaaS-like, enabling easy payments and certain tools to make event creators' business more efficient, and we're layering in more of the traditional marketplace value prop of demand, driving more ticket sales for these event creators. I would say it's got a ways to go to be working really well. (00:57:29): What does working really well look like? It's when the marketplace model unlocks those cross-side network effects that make it easier to grow. Event creators, when Eventbrite started, they would just go do their own marketing to bring people to Eventbrite to transact on their events that they had listed there. Now Eventbrite drives 25% of the ticket sales itself, and that percentage is growing faster than-
turns.zh: 那是 OpenTable。看，这绝对是我们在 Eventbrite 在做的战略，我们从更偏 SaaS 的东西起步，赋能轻松支付和某些工具让活动创建者的生意更高效，然后我们在叠加更传统的市场价值主张——需求，给这些活动创建者驱动更多售票。我会说它还有段路要走，才能真的好用。（00:57:29）真用好用长什么样？就是当市场模型解锁那些跨边网络效应，让增长更容易。活动创建者，Eventbrite 起步时，他们会自己去营销、把人带到 Eventbrite、在他们列在那的活动上交易。现在 Eventbrite 自己驱动了 25% 的售票，而且那个百分比增长得比——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh, wow. That's amazing.
turns.zh: 哦，哇。那太惊人了。

turns.speaker: Casey Winters
turns.en: Yeah. It's growing faster than the rest of the business, which is great, but it probably needs to be closer to 50% to unlock those really cross-side network effects. That would mean that creators start selecting Eventbrite because of all the demand Eventbrite has versus the quality of the SaaS tools. That's obviously something we're working on. Faire is a company I advised more recently that I think has unlocked this model in the reverse, where Faire is a wholesale marketplace between independent retailers and brands so that you could sell products at these retailers, like a boutique in your local neighborhood. (00:58:29): Faire built the marketplace first, and then it later built a SaaS tool that allowed the brands to onboard their current retailers into the platform and get better terms on payments and free returns. It didn't charge anything to use the SaaS tool for any rebookings that happened through that platform. What that did is it onboarded more independent retailers that they could cross-sell to other brands without needing to use a sales team. When they cross-sold, of course, Faire did take their percentage on those transactions. I think that model's worked out really well, and Faire has grown quite quickly.
turns.zh: 对。它增长得比业务其他部分快，这很好，但它大概需要接近 50% 才能解锁那些真正的跨边网络效应。那意味着创建者开始因为 Eventbrite 的所有需求、而不是 SaaS 工具的质量，去选 Eventbrite。那显然是我们正在做的。Faire 是我更近期顾问的一家公司，我觉得它在反向解锁了这个模型——Faire 是独立零售商和品牌之间的批发市，这样你能在这些零售商那卖产品，比如你邻里的精品店。（00:58:29）Faire 先建了市场，然后后来建了个 SaaS 工具，让品牌能把他们现在的零售商接进平台、拿到更好的付款条款和免费退货。对任何通过那个平台发生的再预订，用它那个 SaaS 工具不收任何费。那做的事是：接进了更多独立零售商，他们能交叉销售给其他品牌，而不需要用销售团队。当他们交叉销售时，当然，Faire 在那些交易上抽了他们的百分比。我觉得那个模型管得真不错，Faire 增长得相当快。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The examples you gave, Eventbrite was a SaaS tool trying to add a marketplace.
turns.zh: 你给的例子，Eventbrite 是个试图加市场的 SaaS 工具。

turns.speaker: Casey Winters
turns.en: Yep.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Faire is an example of a marketplace adding a SaaS tool. Is the takeaway there that it's, in your experience, it's generally more ... You're going to have a better time if you're a marketplace adding a SaaS tool versus the other way around?
turns.zh: Faire 是个加 SaaS 工具的市场例子。那里的结论是，在你经验里，一般是更……如果你是个加 SaaS 工具的市场，比反过来，你会过得更顺？

turns.speaker: Casey Winters
turns.en: Yeah. I think that's right. I think, I don't know when it was. Just maybe like 2015 or whatever. A bunch of investors started writing about SaaS to marketplace transitions, and that's the transition Eventbrite's going through. It's going to work, but it's hard. It's not replicable for a lot of other SaaS businesses. You need to have a direct relationship with your customers' customers, first off. Those customers need to have needs beyond that single supplier. (00:59:50): Usually, it's like a discovery value prop for other suppliers, and you need to build this totally new skill set to build tools for your customer's customer, who is very different from your current customer. Whereas, marketplace is that added SaaS component. It's a customer acquisition tool like Faire, or a workflow, or a retention tool to increase retention or reduce disintermediation. I think you'll see that be a lot more common approach and much more replicable.
turns.zh: 对。我觉得那是对的。我觉得，我不知道是什么时候。大概 2015 或随便。一堆投资人开始写从 SaaS 到市场的转型，而那就是 Eventbrite 在经历的转型。它会管用，但它难。它对很多其他 SaaS 生意不可复制。首先，你需要跟你客户的客户有直接关系。那些客户需要有超出那个单一供应商的需求。（00:59:50）通常，是对其他供应商的发现价值主张，而你需要建这套全新的技能，去为你客户的客户建工具——那跟你现在的客户非常不同。而市场那个加的 SaaS 组件，是个客户获取工具，像 Faire，或者一个工作流，或者一个留存工具去提升留存或降低去中介化。我觉得你会看到那是个常见得多、也可复制得多的做法。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is this just rooted in the fact that marketplaces are incredibly hard, no matter whether you start with them or whether you add them? Is that the root of the issue here?
turns.zh: 这只是扎根于这个事实：市场极难，无论你是起步就有它们、还是后来加上？这是这问题的根吗？

turns.speaker: Casey Winters
turns.en: I think that's a good way to frame it. If you're building a startup in 2023 and you're like, "Oh, I'm going to build a SaaS business, and then five years later, I'm going to build this marketplace business on top of that," it's kind of like it's going to take a long time for you to de-risk the hardest part of that strategy. Whereas, if you get the hard part done upfront, it opens up a lot of amazing adjacencies, different ways to grow. I think there's definitely truth in that statement.
turns.zh: 我觉得那是框住它的好方式。如果你在 2023 年建初创，像"哦，我要建个 SaaS 生意，然后五年后，我在那上面建这个市场生意，"有点像，要花很久才能为那战略最难的部分去风险。而如果你把难的部分 upfront 做完，它打开很多惊人的邻接、不同的增长方式。我觉得那陈述里绝对有真相。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The takeaway here is that if you're trying to add a marketplace, it's going to be very hard. You shared a couple things, a couple attributes that tell you that maybe it might work. Maybe just share those again real quick.
turns.zh: 这里的结论是，如果你想加市场，会非常难。你分享了几件事、几个属性告诉你也许它会管用。也许快速再分享一下那些。

turns.speaker: Casey Winters
turns.en: Take Square, or Substack, or Patreon, or Eventbrite. All of these are examples of SaaS businesses that in providing a SaaS service, deal with the customer and the customer's customer. That makes it a lot easier because you already have a relationship. They already know your brand, whereas, Stripe, we buy things. We don't know if we're buying it through Stripe. It's just a SaaS tool that's white labeled on the backend. We have no idea. I think that's the first element. There's a lot of businesses that look like that, but it is a subset of SaaS businesses that look like that. (01:01:38): Then secondly, those customers that you're building a relationship with, they need to have a reason to transact with more than one of your current customers on the supply side, so if you're always going to use that same supplier, there's no need for me to show you the rest of the inventory. (01:01:57): Basically, all marketplaces win on, like we mentioned, selection and you needing selection. Then there's, of course, the marketplaces that win with standardization of like, I can get it at any time. It might be from different people, but I know that Uber car is going to be there in five minutes, or whatever. I don't care as much who the driver is. One of those has to be there. You just find in a lot of these examples, there isn't really that much of a discovery need for who the demand side would be in this theoretical marketplace when you dig into it.
turns.zh: 拿 Square、或者 Substack、或者 Patreon、或者 Eventbrite。所有这些都是 SaaS 生意的例子，在提供 SaaS 服务时，既打交道客户、也打交道的客户的客户。那让它容易得多，因为你已经有关系了。他们已经知道你的品牌，而 Stripe，我们买东西。我们不知道我们是不是通过 Stripe 买的。它只是后端白标的 SaaS 工具。我们完全不知道。我觉得那是第一元素。有很多生意那样，但那只是那样看起来像的 SaaS 生意的一个子集。（01:01:38）然后第二，你在建关系的那些客户，他们需要有理由跟供给侧不止一个你现在的客户交易，所以如果你永远会用同一个供应商，我没必要给你看剩下的库存。（01:01:57）基本上，所有市场赢在，像我们提的，选择、以及你需要选择。然后当然，有靠标准化赢的市场，像我能随时拿到。它可能来自不同的人，但我知道那辆 Uber 五分钟会到，随便。我不太 care 谁开的。那些里得有一个在那。你就在很多这些例子里发现，当你深挖，这个理论上的市场对需求侧是谁，其实没那么多发现需求。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It might be helpful just to define what makes it a marketplace. In my eyes, it's you're driving demand through supply. That's like the nuance, right? Because otherwise, you're just a tool that they're using to do something they want to do.
turns.zh: 定义一下什么让它成为市场，也许有帮助。在我眼里，是你通过供给驱动需求。那是微妙处，对吧？因为否则，你只是他们用来做他们想做的事的工具。

turns.speaker: Casey Winters
turns.en: Yeah. Exactly, right. It's like the primary value prop of why supply signs up is that you're going to bring them extra business. If you have customer, buyers and sellers, but the primary reason supply signs up is for tooling or payments like how Eventbrite started, that's not really a marketplace. I call it a SaaS-like network. Some people might just call it a SaaS business, a payments business, whatever the case may be, but it doesn't really have those cross-side network effects that we associate with marketplaces.
turns.zh: 对。完全，对。就像供给侧注册的主要原因，是你打算给他们带额外生意。如果你有客户、买卖两边，但供给侧注册的主要原因是工具或付款——像 Eventbrite 起步那样——那不是真市场。我叫它 SaaS 式网络。有些人也许就叫它 SaaS 生意、付款生意，无论哪种，但它确实没有那些我们跟市场关联的跨边网络效应。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What this makes me think about is Patreon and Substack. Interestingly, when I was looking at early Patreon days, what I understand is they wanted to be a marketplace. They wanted to be a place where artists come. They collect payment, and then people can discover artists to patronize. What they found is nobody needed ... That wasn't a problem anyone had.
turns.zh: 这让我想到 Patreon 和 Substack。有意思的是，我看早期 Patreon 的日子时，我理解的是他们想做市场。他们想做个艺术家来的地方。他们收付款，然后人们能发现艺术家去赞助。他们发现的是，没人需要……那不是任何人有过的问题。

turns.speaker: Casey Winters
turns.en: Exactly, exactly.
turns.zh: 完全，完全。

turns.en: I'm not looking for- [inaudible 01:03:31]
turns.zh: 我不是在找——[听不清 01:03:31]

turns.en: I'm not looking for other people to donate money to. Same with GoFundMe, right?
turns.zh: 我不是在找别人捐钱给。GoFundMe 也一样，对吧？

turns.en: With that story in mind, when I was chatting with the Substack people early on, it was like this is exactly what you're going to run into. No one's sitting around looking for more newsletters to subscribe to, but shockingly, they've actually pulled it off.

turns.speaker: Casey Winters
turns.en: Yeah.

turns.en: They have a really wild network effect going now and marketplace.

turns.speaker: Casey Winters
turns.en: I've been very impressed with what they've built. I don't know if I'd call it a marketplace yet, but I think they were able to abstract a way, the version of what you just said to something that was actually useful, which is, yes, I don't want more emails to subscribe to, but I do ... I am fundamentally interested in more articles relevant to my interests. No one has really solved that super well. (01:04:15): Twitter was a very hacky form of that, where I follow you and then I see you when you post a new blog because you tell everyone on Twitter you posted a new blog, but it isn't built for that. Whereas the Substack reader will now allow me to be like, "Ah, yeah. Sure, I'll subscribe," so I really like what they've done. It'll be interesting to see how big a business that is and how it all plays out. I think their execution has been really solid.
turns.zh: 我对他们建的印象很深。我不知道我会不会就叫它市场，但我觉得他们能把你刚说的那个版本，抽象成真有用的东西——也就是，对，我不想订阅更多邮件，但我确实……我对跟我兴趣更相关的更多文章，有根本的兴趣。没人真解决得好。（01:04:15）Twitter 是那种很 hacky 的形式，我关注你，然后你发新博客时我看到你，因为你告诉 Twitter 所有人你发了新博客，但它不是为那个建的。而 Substack reader 现在会让我像"啊，对。当然，我订阅，"所以我真喜欢他们做的。会很有意思看那是个多大的生意、怎么全展开。我觉得他们的执行真扎实。

turns.en: Awesome. I feel the same way. I also wasn't sure whether it makes ... it's worth calling a marketplace, but for whatever it's worth, 80% of my new signups are coming from Substack's network, the recommendations feature and their onboarding, things like that. Like-
turns.zh: 太棒了。我也这么觉得。我也不确定它算不算……值不值得叫市场，但无论值不值，我 80% 的新注册来自 Substack 的网络，推荐功能和他们的 onboarding，之类。像——

turns.speaker: Casey Winters
turns.en: Do you think that's unique to you because you're already a top one percenter Substacker? Or is that a meaningful number for new-ish players? If I finally switch my email list to Substack, which has been on my list for a long time, that probably won't be the same percentage for me, right?
turns.zh: 你觉得那对你独特吗，因为你已经是 Substack 前百分之一的人？还是对新玩家也是个有意义的数？如果我终于把我的邮件列表转到 Substack——那在我清单上很久了——那大概不会对我也是同个百分比，对吧？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Absolutely not. Yeah, no, I think there's definitely, if you're there first and people know of you, more people will recommend you. I think, over time, more and more people start to recommend you. I think they released a stat that something like 40% of their new users are coming from a recommendation, or new signups or something like that. It's pretty widely happening, but I don't know how much-
turns.zh: 绝对不是。对，不，我觉得肯定有，如果你先在那、人们知道你，更多人会推荐你。我觉得随时间，越来越多人开始推荐你。我觉得他们发过个统计，大概 40% 的新用户来自推荐，或新注册之类。它相当广泛地发生，但我不知道多少——

turns.speaker: Casey Winters
turns.en: That's excellent.
turns.zh: 那极好。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: ... of that is just the top 10, so it's pretty incredible. It was a really innovative feature and good job, Substack. We had a product on this podcast talking about that exact feature for a whole hour, if you're interested.
turns.zh: ……那只是前 10%，所以挺不可思议的。那是个真创新的功能，干得好 Substack。我们这播客有期产品聊了那个确切功能整整一小时，如果你有兴趣。

turns.speaker: Casey Winters
turns.en: Awesome.
turns.zh: 太棒了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. Final question, and then we have our very exciting lightening round. This is around consumer companies and consumer subscription companies. I know you work with a lot of founders that are building consumer subscription companies, and just consumer startups in general.
turns.zh: 好。最后一个问题，然后我们到超刺激的闪电回合。这是关于消费公司和消费订阅公司。我知道你跟很多建消费订阅公司、以及一般消费初创的创始人合作。

turns.speaker: Casey Winters
turns.en: Yep.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You often tell me how they're incredibly hard to build into thriving businesses. Can you just talk about why consumer subscription startups are so hard and products are so hard?
turns.zh: 你常告诉我它们有多难做成蓬勃的生意。你能讲讲为什么消费订阅初创这么难、产品这么难？

turns.speaker: Casey Winters
turns.en: I feel like we're making this quite a downer podcast, Lenny, but-
turns.zh: 我觉得我们在把这做成个挺丧的播客，Lenny，但——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This is, people need to hear the truth. There's a lot of happy talk out there, and a lot of posts, "Here's how you do this."
turns.zh: 这是，人们需要听真相。外面有很多快乐 talk，很多帖子"这是你怎么做的。"

turns.speaker: Casey Winters
turns.en: Sure.
turns.zh: 当然。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Sometimes, you can't.
turns.zh: 有时，你就是做不到。

turns.speaker: Casey Winters
turns.en: I think in order to understand these businesses, you have to start with, why do investors like B2B SaaS? Why do they like B2B subscription? I think the way most people respond to that question, they say like, "Oh, predictable revenue, right?" It's like, ah, sure. That's cool and all, but I think that's actually not the most important. I'd argue there's two great attributes of B2B SaaS. One is that businesses are more predictable in how well they're routine. They're rational. You can understand who are good versus bad businesses for your product, as well as which ones are going to grow versus go out of business. (01:06:53): More importantly, the second thing that's great about B2B SaaS is net dollar retention. What is net dollar retention if you don't work at SaaS? Well, as a SaaS company, some of your customers are going to churn. Some of your customers are going to stay. Normally, normally outside of potentially current macroeconomic conditions with all the layoffs, when customers do stick around, they tend to spend more. Either they buy more seats if you're a seat-based model, or they use the product more if you're a usage model. The SaaS company just makes more money in year two, year three, et cetera. (01:07:27): Consumer subscription just doesn't have any of these benefits. Consumers are way less predictable. They tend to retain worse than businesses, and they also don't have net dollar retention characteristics. If the user retains paying you in year two, you probably making the same amount that you made from them in year one, not more. What that means is you need higher user-based retention than B2B SaaS businesses with more unpredictable users, and it's a lot higher than, I think, founders tend to think. We're talking annual retention that needs to be north of 60, perhaps even 70%. (01:08:04): You look at who's actually been able to do that at scale, and it's a really small list. Netflix in the U.S., Amazon Prime, Spotify, Duolingo, I think, is emerging as one of these players that's making it work. When you look at how they do it, they're either doing it with massive OPEX and economies of scale, or through a network effect, or some other bespoke growth loop that's not that easy to replicate. Duolingo has a strong data network effect. The lessons get better the more people use it. Beek, the company I'm on the board of has a cross-side network effect between creators who create the content and the listeners, and the creators bring a lot of distribution from their existing social networks to bring new people in the app to listen. Netflix and Amazon, they spend billions of dollars on content. (01:08:58): I think the default path of like, "I'm going to spend money on paid acquisition. I'm going to retain half of my audience year-over-year." That's just a path to go on eventually. I think what's interesting about these businesses is you can model it so you can learn when it's going to happen. You can learn when the retention dips, and when you can no longer profitably acquire users. If you want to look at a model in real time, just look at Blue Apron. The company raised $300 million in an IPO that valued it at $2 billion. It's worth $50 million today on the New York Stock Exchange. (01:09:35): I think people understand now, if they didn't before, that paid acquisition tends to get worse as you scale. You target the best customers first. They have great conversion, great retention, and then as you expand your targeting of new customers, every one of those metrics gets worse until it's no longer profitable. Maybe two years from now, it may be be five years from now, but eventually, it'll be no longer profitable. What network effects allow you to do is they allow your product to get better faster than the customers you target get worse, normally, through increased selection, like some of the examples we gave with DoorDash and others.
turns.zh: 我觉得为了理解这些生意，你得从：为什么投资人喜欢 B2B SaaS？为什么他们喜欢 B2B 订阅？我觉得大多数人对那问题的回应，像"哦，可预测营收，对吧？"就像，啊，当然。那酷归酷，但我觉得那其实不是最重要的。我会说 B2B SaaS 有两个好属性。一是企业更可预测，他们日常多规律。他们理性。你能理解谁对你的产品是好 vs 坏企业，以及哪些会增长 vs 倒闭。（01:06:53）更重要的是，B2B SaaS 第二好的事是净收入留存率（NDR）。如果你不在 SaaS 工作，NDR 是什么？作为 SaaS 公司，你有些客户会流失。有些会留。通常，通常除了可能当前宏观经济条件加所有裁员，当客户真留下来，他们倾向花更多。要么你是基于座位模型他们买更多座位，要么你是基于用量模型他们用更多产品。SaaS 公司就在第二年、第三年等赚更多钱。（01:07:27）消费订阅就是没有任何这些好处。消费者远不可预测。他们比企业留存差，而且他们也没有 NDR 特性。如果用户第二年还付你钱，你大概赚的跟第一年从他们那赚的一样多，不是更多。那意味着你需要比 B2B SaaS 生意更高、用户更不可预测的留存，而且它比我觉得创始人倾向想的，高得多。我们说的是年度留存得在 60 以上，也许甚至 70%。（01:08:04）你看谁真能在规模上做到，那是极短的名单。Netflix 在美国，Amazon Prime，Spotify，Duolingo，我觉得正作为一个做成这事的人冒出来。你看他们怎么做，他们要么靠海量运营开支和规模经济，要么靠网络效应，要么某些别的定制增长环，那不太容易复制。Duolingo 有强数据网络效应。越多人用，课越好。Beek，我董事会的那家，在创建内容的人和听众之间有跨边网络效应，而创作者从他们现有社交网络带很多分发，把新人带进 app 听。Netflix 和 Amazon，他们花几十亿在内容上。（01:08:58）我觉得那种默认路径，像"我要花钱在付费获取上。我要逐年留住一半我的受众。"那只是条最终走向尽头的路。我觉得这些生意有意思的是，你能建模，这样你能学到它什么时候会发生。你能学到留存什么时候跌、什么时候你不再能盈利地获取用户。如果你想实时看个模型，就看 Blue Apron。那公司在 IPO 融了 3 亿、估值 20 亿。今天在纽交所值 5000 万。（01:09:35）我觉得人们现在懂了，如果他们之前不懂，付费获取往往随你规模化变得更差。你先 targeting 最好的客户。他们转化好、留存好，然后随你扩展对新客户的 targeting，每个那些指标都变差，直到不再盈利。也许两年后，也许五年后，但最终，会不再盈利。网络效应让你能做的，是让产品变好得比你 targeting 的客户变差更快，通常，通过增加的选择，像我们给 DoorDash 和其他的几个例子。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This is such a cool topic. I actually have a post about this that I recalled now as you're talking about it. Just to double-click on the retention point and it's like, freaks you out when you really get into it. That say your retention is like 70% cohort retention for a year. I forget the math, but every three or four years, you basically have to rebuild your entire user base because it just, it keeps trickling out, so your growth just has to continue-
turns.zh: 这话题太酷了。我其实有篇关于这个的帖子，你聊时我想起来了。就深挖留存点，它像，当你真钻进去会吓到你。假设你的留存是一年 70% 的队列留存。我忘数学了，但每三四你基本得重建你整个用户基础，因为它就一直涓涓流出，所以你的增长就不得不继续——

turns.speaker: Casey Winters
turns.en: It's mind-boggling. You run out of humans. Yeah, it's really hard. If you can retain people incredibly well, meaning those people just never churn, yeah, you've got a great business, but look at the effort the companies that have done that are doing to do that. Spotify doesn't make profit. Netflix, Amazon just spend so much money to try to do that. How replicable is that for a startup? I'd rather say like, "Let's try and get some network effects involved here. Let's get our customer acquisition cost to zero. Let's think about other ways to monetize because this alone feels like [inaudible 01:11:07]."
turns.zh: 它令人难以置信。你用光人类。对，真难。如果你能极好地留住人，意思是那些人从不流失，对，你有个好生意，但看做成那事的公司花多大精力去做。Spotify 不赚钱。Netflix、Amazon 就花那么多钱去试做那。对初创多可复制？我倒想说"咱们试着在这搞些网络效应。让咱们把客户获取成本弄到零。让咱们想别的变现方式，因为这单独感觉像[听不清 01:11:07]。"

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This is also why a lot of these companies pivot to B2B. They realize they're not going to get anywhere with B2C. The other lesson I took away ... Because I interviewed a lot of these early B2C subscription app founders and employees, and I think about companies like Grammarly, Duolingo, Noom. Forget. There are a few more. One of the other trends across them all is they're all very efficient and very small for a long time because they needed time to figure out how to make anything work and then just continue to stay small and super scrappy.
turns.zh: 这也是为什么很多这些公司 pivot 到 B2B。他们意识到 B2C 走不远。我拿走的另一个教训……因为我采访了很多这些早期 B2C 订阅 app 的创始人和员工，我想到像 Grammarly、Duolingo、Noom 的公司。忘了。还有几个。跨它们所有的另一个趋势是，他们长期都极高效、极小，因为他们需要时间搞懂怎么让任何事管用，然后就继续保持小、超 scrappy。

turns.speaker: Casey Winters
turns.en: I think that's a great point. It was an interesting case study between Calm and Headspace. Because Calm remained like 10 people forever.
turns.zh: 我觉得那是个好点。Calm 和 Headspace 之间是个有意思的案例研究。因为 Calm 永远像 10 个人。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow.
turns.zh: 哇。

turns.speaker: Casey Winters
turns.en: Headspace had gone into like hundreds of people. Calm basically never lost money, and that allowed them to pivot easier during massive changes, like app tracking transparency threw a wrench into all paid acquisition. If you're not losing money, cool. You have time to figure out how to grow again, but if that increases your burn by like $100 million, you have a lot more of a panic on your hands.
turns.zh: Headspace 已经到了几百人。Calm 基本从没亏钱，而那让他们在巨大变化中更容易 pivot，像 App 追踪透明度给所有付费获取扔了个扳手。如果你不亏钱，酷。你有时间搞懂怎么再增长，但如果那把你的烧钱增加 1 亿，你手上有多得多恐慌。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Maybe just to tie the loop, tie the knot, close the thread on this topic, if you're a B2C subscription founder, what would be some takeaways that you would want to put in their head to think about how to maybe survive?
turns.zh: 也许就收个尾、打个结、关掉这个话题的线，如果你是个 B2C 订阅创始人，你会有什么结论想放进他们脑袋，去想怎么也许活下来？

turns.speaker: Casey Winters
turns.en: Yeah, so if what your plan is is to use paid acquisition on top of a freemium model to get a percentage of people to convert, and hopefully, stick around forever, I'd pivot right now. It's like, I just cannot see it working. How do you pivot? Well, how do you make it social so that people are bringing in other people? How do you get a supply side to the content, or education, or whatever you're building and make it in the supply side's interest to refer people? (01:12:55): You have to do something that's either building some more organic growth loops into the business, or building network effects into the business, or else we could go spend two hours and model out exactly when you're going to run out of money. It's just that predictable. A lot of founders don't like to hear it when I tell them that, but I'd rather them hear it now than learn it three years from now.
turns.zh: 对，所以如果你的计划是在免费增值模型上用付费获取，去让一定比例的人转化，并希望永远留下，我现在就 pivot。就像，我就是看不出它管用。怎么 pivot？嗯，你怎么让它社交，让人们带别人进来？你怎么拿到内容、或教育、或你建的东西的供给侧，并让它符合供给侧利益去推荐人？（01:12:55）你得做某种要么把更多有机增长环建进生意、要么把网络效应建进生意的事，否则我们能花两小时精确建模出你什么时候会把钱烧光。就那么可预测。很多创始人不爱听我说这个，但我宁愿他们现在听，而不是三年后学。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Well, we've reached our very exciting lightening round. I'm just going to dive right in. What are two or three books that you've most recommended to other people?
turns.zh: 好，我们到超刺激的闪电回合了。我直接跳进去。你最经常推荐给别人的是哪两三本书？

turns.speaker: Casey Winters
turns.en: Definitely The Goal by Eliyahu Goldratt, which explains how my brain works, pretty well. Thinking, Fast and Slow by Danny Kahneman. I took a lot of the behavioral economics classes in my MBA program, and then his book came out the year after, so I just absorbed it as quick as possible.
turns.zh: 绝对是 Eliyahu Goldratt 的《目标》（The Goal），它解释我脑子怎么运作，相当好。《思考，快与慢》（Thinking, Fast and Slow） by Danny Kahneman。我在 MBA 项目里上了很多行为经济课，然后他的书在次年出了，所以我尽快吸收了它。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Was he your professor, or that was just the topic?
turns.zh: 他是你教授吗，还是那只是话题？

turns.speaker: Casey Winters
turns.en: Some of his pupils were professors of mine, yeah.
turns.zh: 他的一些学生是我的教授，对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. Very cool.
turns.zh: 惊人。超酷。

turns.speaker: Casey Winters
turns.en: Then the third is a book called Profit from the Core by Chris Zook.
turns.zh: 然后第三本是 Chris Zook 的《从核心盈利》（Profit from the Core）。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. That's a new one. I love when there's new books being added to the collection.
turns.zh: 惊人。那是本新的。我爱有新书加进收藏。

turns.speaker: Casey Winters
turns.en: There you go.
turns.zh: 给你。

turns.en: Okay. Next question. Favorite recent movie or TV show?
turns.zh: 好。下一个问题。最近最爱的电影或剧？

turns.en: Well, Party Down just came back and that's like-
turns.zh: 嗯，Party Down 刚回归，那像——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I've been watching that.
turns.zh: 我一直在看那个。

turns.speaker: Casey Winters
turns.en: That's one of my favorite-
turns.zh: 那是我最爱的——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'd never heard of it.
turns.zh: 我从没听过它。

turns.speaker: Casey Winters
turns.en: It's one of my favorite comedies of all time. Yeah, go back-
turns.zh: 那是我有史以来最爱的喜剧之一。对，回去——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Cool.
turns.zh: 酷。

turns.speaker: Casey Winters
turns.en: Go back and watch the first couple seasons if you haven't.

turns.en: That's what I've been doing. That's what I've been doing.

turns.en: Okay. Great, great. Other things like The Last of Us is great. I really enjoyed the video games. Severance is great. Station Eleven is great. I think it really holds up well. I really enjoyed that one.
turns.zh: 好。棒，棒。别的像《最后生还者》（The Last of Us）很棒。我超爱那电子游戏。《人生切割术》（Severance）很棒。《第十一站》（Station Eleven）很棒。我也爱那本书，但我觉得那拍得真不错。电影，最近没真出很多好电影，但我重看了 90 年代的《Kicking and Screaming》。我觉得它真的经得起时间。我不知道你们多少听过它，但它是关于一群大学孩子毕业了，但他们就决定不离校、不开始他们的人生，就赖在校园里。我超爱那个。

turns.speaker: Lenny

(01:15:09): Two more questions. What's something relatively minor you've changed in your product development process, or maybe that you've recommended people change that has had a tremendous impact on people's ability to execute?
turns.zh: 惊人。我们有个喝酒游戏，任何时候有人提 Last of Us，所以如果你开车上班路上在通勤听你播客，拿点咖啡或你有的啥。（01:15:09）还有两个问题。你产品流程里改过什么相对小的东西，或者也许你推荐人改的、对人们执行能力有巨大影响的？

turns.speaker: Casey Winters
turns.en: I preach cross-functional teams and alignment pretty aggressively, so how to get people from all the different functions aligned on the same OKRs and working together. I used to say like, "Look, if someone in that cross-functional team is pulling rank, it means something's fucked up on the team." (01:15:39): Something we started doing more recently at both Eventbrite and Whatnot is just designating the person on the cross-functional team who drives the project. At Eventbrite, we call it the driver. At Whatnot, we call it the DRI, directly responsible individual. Once that person makes the call, it's disagree and commit time. There's no escalation path. If you're not the DRI and you're on the team and they made the call, all right. It's time to sign up and go forward on that decision. If they made the wrong decision later, okay, we'll learn once we ship.
turns.zh: 我相当激进地宣扬跨职能团队和对齐，所以怎么让来自不同职能的人对齐在同一 OKR 上、一起工作。我以前说像"看，如果那个跨职能团队里有人摆资历，意味着团队里有什么 fucked up 了。"（01:15:39）我们最近在 Eventbrite 和 Whatnot 都开始做的一件事，就是指定那个跨职能团队里驱动项目的人。在 Eventbrite，我们叫它 driver（驾驶员）。在 Whatnot，我们叫它 DRI，直接责任人（directly responsible individual）。一旦那个人做了决定，就是"不同意但执行"时间。没有升级路径。如果你不是 DRI 而你在团队里、他们做了决定，行。是时候签上、往前走那个决定。如果他们后来做了错决定，行，我们发布后学。

turns.zh: 最后一个问题。我很爱你在你自己 newsletter 和博客里做的，是你分享你在听什么。你最近在听什么？

turns.en: Sure. Kelela recently came out with her second album, Raven, which is really great. I've been listening to that. Orbital came out with a new album called Optimal Delusion that's been pretty good. Then an oldie but goodie is De La Soul's music finally came out on Spotify, and the Stakes Is High is one of my favorite hip hop albums ever, so I've been jamming to that.
turns.zh: 当然。Kelela 最近出了她第二张专辑《Raven》，真棒。我一直在听那个。Orbital 出了张新专辑叫《Optimal Delusion》，相当好。然后个老但好的，De La Soul 的音乐终于上 Spotify 了，而《Stakes Is High》是我有史以来最爱的嘻哈专辑之一，所以我一直在嗨那个。

turns.zh: 我博客远没你频繁，在 caseyaccidental.com。你能在 Twitter @onecaseman 找到我。对，就传递下去。帮你公司建更好的产品、更好的生意。那是我全在乎的。
